Mr. Speaker, Canadians pride themselves on their educational institutions and their commitment to international aid, yet somehow these two concerns do not get together. Canada gives only 1,500 scholarships to students from developing countries, which is less than 1 per cent of our ODA budget. Britain, by comparison, gives 20,000 scholarships.
Of the limited aid we do give, little goes to students from the poorest countries. For those students who do get to come here, there are bureaucratic hassles to endure over visa renewals. Groups assisting international students suggest we could do much more by providing up to 10,000 scholarships, for example, and simplifying bureaucratic procedures.
Most of the non-Canadian students at Canadian universities and colleges are not on scholarships but are paying their own way, aiding the Canadian economy by doing so. Surely we could be doing more to making our post-secondary institutions accessible to those who cannot afford the fees and, in the meantime, winning friends for Canada and partners in our development.

Mr. Speaker, on February 16, 1918, Lithuania became an independent democratic nation. Lithuania lost that treasured status in 1940 when the Soviet Union invaded the Baltic States.
Freedom has always been an important aspect of Lithuanian life. In the 1890s, the first Lithuanians to arrive in Canada

February 13, 1987
were refugees from Czarist Russia. In 1945 Lithuanians were fleeing the ravages of two occupiers, the Nazis and the Soviets. Both waves of immigrants from Lithuania have made a significant contribution to the growth and development of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Inna Meiman, one of several Soviet Jewish cancer patients whom Montreal physician Dr. Gerald Batist has championed, was
finally allowed to leave the Soviet Union after years of trying. She was allowed to leave for treatment purposes only, having to leave behind her husband and son. But the exit visa for treatment purposes really came too late.

Mr. Speaker, in March of 1985 a joint committee of Parliament brought to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans the fact that the international Pacific halibut regulations were illegal. He did nothing.
The committee called on the Minister on February 6, 1986, to revoke the regulations and have them legally drafted. The committee pointed out:
We also wish for a formal assurance that, pending the formal revocation of the Regulations, fishery officers will be instructed not to enforce them and that no one has or will be charged for a breach of the Regulations.
Again, the Minister did nothing.
Article 111(2) of the Convention as passed by Parliament confers the regulation-making powers on the commission, not on the Minister. Regina v. Feraco, 1965, confirms that regulations made by the Minister in their present form mean that they are null and void.
The Minister has been and is as of this date breaching an international agreement with the United States. From 1959 to 1984 the regulations were passed legally.
Since part of the B.C. halibut fishery begins in two weeks, I call upon the Minister to put in place legal regulations to protect the fishery and the rights of B.C. commercial and sports fishermen.
February 13, 1987

subsubtopic: AGREEMENT TO CLEAN UP NIAGARA RIVER TOXIC POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that on February 4 the principal U.S. and Canadian government agencies responsible for environmental protection signed an agreement for the clean-up of the Niagara River. The agreement calls on the four participating agencies to report to the public every six months on the progress being made to reduce toxic chemicals from entering the Niagara River. Most important, it calls for a target reduction level of 50 per cent for loadings of persistent toxic chemicals from sources on both sides of the Niagara River by 1996. This is a tremendous step forward. I congratulate all parties to the agreement but, in particular, our federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) for his leadership.
My constituents will be particularly pleased because, for 20 years, they watched while the federal Liberals did absolutely nothing for the toxic chemical clean-up of the Niagara River. They know they did nothing. That has now changed under this Government.

subsubtopic: AGREEMENT DESIRED BETWEEN UNITED STATES AND U.S.S.R. ON COMPLETE BANNING OF NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are receiving an increasing number of letters and comments on nuclear testing.
As we all know, Canada is against the use of nuclear arms and the testing of such arms on its territory, and this position has been very well received.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SERVICE IN RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, postal service is a vital link for rural communities in Canada. Rural communities consider access to stamp purchase, money orders, parcel service, et cetera not only a right but an absolute necessity. Green boxes only offer a receptacle for incoming mail, and ignore the necessary service required for outgoing mail.
Recent announcements by Post Office Ministers of the Government to give 90 days for rural residents to be surveyed concerning their options are not real consultation, but an information and public relations exercise to let people know what the predetermined new lowers levels of service will be. The options are either green boxes or complete abandonment of the postal point altogether.
There has been no change in post office policy in rural areas. The existing policy continues. Rural residents served by small postal stations receive no reassurance from the Government's actions and policy on the Post Office.

subtopic: AIDS DISEASE-LACK OF TESTING OF PROSPECTIVE IMMIGRANTS
AIDS DISEASE-LACK OF TESTING OF PROSPECTIVE IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the present time anyone suffering from AIDS is not admissible as an immigrant to Canada. Equally, no mandatory testing for AIDS is required of anyone applying for admission to this country. AIDS is a highly infectious disease, and there is great public concern over it. Many provinces are implementing educational programs. Twenty-three per cent of the cases of AIDS in Ontario have involved people originating from outside Canada.
Surely it is reasonable to expect that the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the Immigration Medical Review Board take another look at the requirements for admission to Canada, and assure the public that every reasonable step is being taken to exclude this disease from our country.

subsubtopic: OZONE LAYER-NEED FOR PROTECTION FROM CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ozone layer in the atmosphere protects us from ultraviolet sun rays and possible skin cancer. Chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, are substances which remove ozone from the atmosphere, and therefore are dangerous. CFCs are used as propellants in aerosol sprays, in foams for insulation, fast-food packaging, coffee cups, in solvents, in cooking sprays, and in medicating sprays. They are released when foam products decay, and when refrigerants are released in the environment.
The reduction in the ozone layer could increase the rate of skin cancer, reduce production of food crops, and enhance the rate of global warming. Canadians should press the Government to ban the use and importation of products containing CFCs. In the meantime, to be part of the solution of the problem, consumers should stop buying foam products containing sprays which use CFCs, and press manufacturers to stop using CFCs in their products.

subsubtopic: POOR PERSONS' LACK OF ACCESS TO SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, banks and other mainstream financial institutions seem to go out of their way to avoid dealing with poor people, according to a study by the National Anti-Poverty Organization. Low-income Canadians are finding that their access to financial services is restricted. Because they are poor, they are unable to obtain services that moderate and upper-income Canadians take for granted. This is not referring to services that could be considered luxuries, but basic services like having social assistance cheques cashed in order to buy food for your family, or obtaining a small loan to replace a refrigerator which has finally given up the ghost.
Mainstream institutions are wary of cashing government cheques, because they fear fraud. Most poor people cannot provide the identification that is needed. The Government should investigate this situation, and make sure all Canadians have equal access to these institutions.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to inform Members of the House that yesterday I filed with the Clerk a Notice of Motion with respect to capital punishment. The wording of the motion is available to Members on today's Order Paper and Notices. I would like to make it clear at the outset that the introduction of this motion does not indicate that the Government supports or opposes the reinstatement of capital punishment.
The intent behind the motion is to permit a full parliamentary debate to be concluded by a free vote on the capital punishment issue. By a free vote I mean that all Members of the Progressive Conservative Party will be free to vote according to their individual wishes and will not be bound by party discipline.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Of course, the opposition Parties can similarly release their Members if they so choose.
Furthermore, the vote will not be considered a matter of confidence by the Government. If the motion is defeated the Government will not consider it a vote of non-confidence.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a commitment to Canadians that a free vote would be held on capital punishment during this Parliament. The Government has examined a number of ways of bringing this question forward. We want an open debate and a truly free vote, and a question formulated in a way to leave all stages of disposition in the hands of Members of the House, outside of the restrictions of the Standing Orders on Private Members' Business.
This issue is a matter of national importance and one that a majority of Canadians want Parliament to consider. It should be debated openly and voted upon in a free manner without

February 13, 1987
Statements by Ministers
impeding the independence of Members of Parliament. We believe the motion introduced today meets those goals.
It is our intention to permit the motion to stand on the Order Paper for a period of time to allow those interested parties in the public to make representations to their Members of Parliament. Indeed, I would expect all Canadians to make their views known through letters, briefs or meetings, or any other form of representation to Members on all sides of the House.
The motion seeks the opinion of the House with respect to the reinstatement of capital punishment. If the motion is defeated, then the matter will end there. If the motion is supported, then the motion will establish a parliamentary committee to prepare and introduce appropriate legislation. While such a practice is permitted under Standing Order 107, it is clearly not a common one. I would remind the House that the McGrath Committee in recommendation 4.12 of its third report stated:
We recommend wider use of parliamentary committees to review draft legislation, to conduct general inquiries when policy choices have not yet been made, and to bring in draft Bills.
In keeping with that recommendation, the motion has been drafted to ensure that all Members of Parliament have the opportunity to have input into the legislation, should the House choose to support reinstatement. This goes to the heart of our efforts to increase the role of the private Member with respect to public policy issues.
As one who has participated in a previous debate on this important issue, I recognize that it is a most difficult and emotional question. I trust that all Members will accept the importance and seriousness of this issue and approach the matter in a thoughtful and reasonable manner. The Government wishes to have a frank debate, a full debate, and a constructive debate. I trust that all Members will examine the question in that spirit.
The motion as presented is amendable. The Government has presented a motion which we feel will leave the House free to shape its decision. The motion now belongs to the House and its Members. The issue is theirs to decide.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, capital punishment is indeed an important and serious issue. We in this House and in the country have been expecting the Government to act on its commitment to introduce a debate on which there will be a free vote with respect to this subject. There is great interest in it. There is also passion.
There are those who feel strongly that the sanctity of life prevents the use of capital punishment by any Government. There are others whose concern with crime and social order lead them as passionately to believe that capital punishment should be reinstated. I call upon both these groups on both sides of the issue to recognize the extent to which they are
being manipulated and abused by this callous and hypocritical Government which introduces this motion at this time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext: For two-and-a-half years you did nothing!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext:
To take an issue as important and serious as this and introduce a motion at this time marks a new low in the performance of the Government. I hope that Canadians will not forget that.
The Government has indicated that the vote is to be a free vote. Yet the motion put forward in the name of a Minister of the Crown supports the principle of capital punishment. I know that in places in the country where the Government can advance its interests by putting this issue forward as a motion of the Government, that is what it is; it is a motion of the Government which supports the reinstatement of capital punishment.
Like the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), I participated in a number of debates on capital punishment. They are not cool, rational or dispassionate discussions. I object strongly, as do members of my Party, to the establishment of a committee which will travel and hear public opinion, which every Member of this House believes has already been heard. Members have made up their minds on this question. The establishment of a committee with a mandate to travel only indicates the attempt of the Government to divert attention from an issue about which opinion is largely settled. No good purpose will be served by the creation of such a committee, other than to create passion, emotion and pressure on all Members of Parliament to vote in one way or another. In any event, this will only distract attention from the most incompetent and perhaps immoral Government in the history of Canada.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext: The Government has hit a new rock bottom with the timing of its motion and the method by which it proposes to proceed.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-FREE VOTE-PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly interesting to see the Government promoting the possibility of greater importance for private Members. It is astonishing to see that the Government does not want to take any leadership. It does not even have an opinion on this most crucial question of life and death which is involved in the issue of capital punishment.
One wonders why capital punishment should be treated as a moral issue, as if there were not other moral issues that we have been addressing, such as poverty and environmental pollution. These are also moral issues. I do not see why this moral issue should be treated in a different fashion from other deeply moral issues that we consider from time to time in the House.
February 13, 1987

The Government is keeping a promise it made in the election campaign. I remind the Government that it also made promises to the arts community with respect to funding, and to students with respect to education, not to mention the sacred trust regarding social programs. The Government promised scientists funding for basic scientific research. These were some of the promises it made.
Yet what is the Government's priority? The Government wants to keep its promise in an area which it knows is highly charged and at a time when its own credibility is sorely at risk. The Government does not look good on account of influence peddling, corruption charges and investigations. But it certainly looks good when murder and capital punishment are being discussed. This is a cheap way for the Government to make itself look good when its own reputation is very much at stake.
The questions as put in the government order are loaded questions. They do not deal with the real issues. If we must have a debate on this subject, I would prefer that the real questions at stake be those before us, namely, the morality of the state in taking life, the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent, the effects in other countries after the elimination of capital punishment, the number of mistakes made in the execution of innocent persons wrongfully convicted of murder and the establishment of the impact upon society generally if capital punishment is reinstated.
I would prefer to see this subject put in a more positive way, if the Government feels it has to keep this promise, of all its promises. Canada has abolished capital punishment, with other enlightened countries. Why not put the question in a positive way, that we will continue this enlightened policy of abolition of capital punishment, and let those who wish to return to the dark ages vote against enlightenment.

Teleglobe Canada

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Privatization) and Minister responsible for the Status of Women) moved
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-38, an Act respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker I welcome this opportunity to introduce the legislation respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, the international telecommunications carrier, authorizing the Government to sell the Crown corporation to Memotec Data Inc. in Montreal.
The transaction is particularly exciting because the dynamic entrepreneurship of Memotec is thus allied with Teleglobe s experience, technology and market access. The resulting combination will certainly attract the attention of the Canadian business world in the years to come.

The privatization of Teleglobe is an important milestone for the Government's privatization process which is itself an integral part of our plans to ensure more prudent management of the whole public sector, including both government Departments and Crown corporations.
Better government management has been a central element of our agenda for economic renewal, an agenda described in the November 1984 document, A New Direction for Canada. The agenda is pragmatic, coherent, and responsible. It is working and it is working well, to the benefit of Canadians.
Our policy recognizes that Crown corporations have played a central role in Canada's economic life. In the main they have served Canadians well, but few Canadians understand just how extensive our network of Crown corporations has become. In 1984 we inherited a vast collection of corporate holdings. Together they employed over 200,000 people, almost as many as in the federal Public Service.
Our policy is to manage better all Crown corporations, to wind down those entities which are no longer required, and to privatize on a case by case basis those Crown corporations where the public interest can be better served through private ownership with public regulation as and when required. This policy is consistent with Canada's traditionally pragmatic approach to public ownership.
We are all prepared to use public ownership when we see it as the best way to serve the public interest. We should all be equally willing to move away from public ownership when that too is in the public interest.
Therefore the Government's approach is sensitive and pragmatic. It is evident that many of the leading spokespersons

February 13, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
on the other side of the House are still wrapped up in the ideology of the 1950s and 1960s and are not aware of how far we have progressed since then.
Essentially the legislation places Teleglobe Canada on the same basis as CP Rail, Bell Canada, CTV, CHUM, or any other of our privately owned, publicly regulated companies.
Some have said that Teleglobe is profitable, a crown jewel, and because it is profitable we should not divest the company to the private sector. Our answer to this plea for the status quo is a simple one. As the late David Lewis once reminded doctrinaire socialists, "you don't have to own an industry in order to have some control over it". Crown ownership is not necessary for Teleglobe to serve the public interest.
In many ways Crown ownership is inhibiting to corporations. For example, Teleglobe is a well managed and profitable company, but it is extremely restricted in what it can do. It cannot be entrepreneurial. It cannot move into new ventures built around its own technological sophistication and its link to international markets. This synergy is precisely on what Memotec proposes to build to develop new products, expanded markets, new exports, and ultimately more jobs for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House is only a means to an end. That end is a privatized, dynamic and growing Teleglobe. The means are perhaps less exciting but just as important. The Bill describes the structure of the transaction, clarifies policies, identifies employee benefits and authorizes the sale.

Clauses 1 through 3 of the Bill are simply definitions. Part II, Clauses 4 through 6, is more substantive. These clauses provide for the creation of a new company organized under the Canada Business Corporations Act. The new Teleglobe will take over the assets of Teleglobe in exchange for securities. The securities, including shares representing 100 per cent of the new Teleglobe, will be sold to Memotec. The only major asset not to be transferred to the new Teleglobe will be the cash on hand in Teleglobe at the time of the sale. This is expected to be approximately $102 million.
We also believe it is sound public policy to ensure that Teleglobe remains Canadian owned and Canadian controlled. Accordingly, foreign ownership will be limited in Part II of the legislation. Non-resident ownership of Teleglobe will be restricted to 20 per cent. Non-resident telecommunications carriers will be totally excluded from Teleglobe's ownership now and in the future. Subsidiaries and affiliates of such nonresident telecommunications carriers will be similarly excluded with specified exceptions.
In addition, limitations are established on the extent to which domestic telecommunications carriers can own shares in the new company. This is designed to prevent the carriers from acquiring effective control of the new company.

The third section of the Bill, clauses 7 to 12, provides that the new corporation has an obligation to provide public telecommunications services such as co-ordinating telecommunications services between Canada and places outside Canada with the telecommunications services of other countries, making use of developments in cable and radio transmission or reception for public telecommunications services between Canada and places outside Canada, and conducting research and development for the purpose of improving telecommunications services.
Teleglobe will be designated to represent Canada in international agreements such as Intelsat, Inmarsat and the Commonwealth Telecommunications Organization, and under Section 15 of Part IV it will also be subject to Government policy directives for a narrow range of national security, foreign relations and international communications policy considerations. But perhaps more important than what the company must do is what it may do. It will not be restricted as to its mandate. It will in the future be free to pursue new business opportunities. This section also designates that the headquarters of the new company shall be located in Montreal.
Part IV of this Bill deals with Teleglobe's regulatory framework by empowering the CRTC to regulate its telecommunications business. By bringing the company under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission, we will ensure that rates and other conditions will be both fair and reasonable into the future for both users and Teleglobe itself. Consumers will benefit from average reductions on overseas telephone charges exceeding 13 per cent in 1988. That will be good news for those many, many Canadians with relatives overseas. More important, the consumer interest will be protected into the future by the CRTC, a protection not present now under Crown ownership.
Later sections of the Bill, namely sections 28, 29 and 30, provide for a transitional regulatory regime to be established immediately. It is under this regime that the Government will require Teleglobe to reduce its rates, and will establish the rules by which rates will be regulated until the end of 1991. The Government will also ensure that Teleglobe remains as Canada's "single-interface" for overseas telecommunications for at least five years. This does not, of itself, provide complete protection for Teleglobe. Some critics have suggested that the telephone companies might attempt to route overseas traffic by way of the U.S. to bypass Teleglobe. However, even if they were to do this, those under federal regulation would require CRTC approval of their actions. It is the policy of our Government that, to the greatest extent feasible, overseas telecommunications shall be provided over Canadian-owned and Canadian controlled facilities. I should say, in fairness as well, that the telephone companies have said publicly that it is not their intention to bypass Teleglobe.
February 13, 1987

Part V, Sections 19 through 22, provides for the sale of Teleglobe. Let me clarify once again the financial implications of this. As Hon. Members know, the gross proceeds of the proposed sale to be received by the Government are $608.3 million, composed of $488.3 million from Memotec, an estimated $102 million in accumulated cash in Teleglobe at the time of the sale, and a special dividend of $18 million in December, 1987. Direct costs are estimated at $7 million, and a contingency reserve of $10 million has been created.
On the accounts of the Government of Canada, the only entry with respect to Teleglobe is a loan for approximately $2 million. Therefore, the impact on the deficit, on the consolidated revenue account, will, in total, be $608.3 million, minus the costs, the contingency reserve and the loan, for a final total of $589.3 million.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Some may ask why the Government did not choose a broad public share issue as a vehicle for Teleglobe's privatization. It is a valid question that certainly deserves an answer. The answer is that we are pursuing privatization on a case by case basis. An in this case, it was our judgment that a strong and dynamic major shareholder will help guide the company during its transition from public ownership to private ownership with regulation. We believe that Memotec will ensure an exciting future for this company. The public interest will be better served by having Memotec establish how it will operate Teleglobe and then go with a public share issue which is already part of its permanent refinancing plan. While a strong majority shareholder is desirable in the case of Teleglobe, public share issues directly by the Government may well be more appropriate for other privatization candidates.
Of course, we fully expect opposition Parties to say otherwise about the benefits of privatization, to take all positions and, like Stephen Leacock's famous horsemen, to ride madly off in all directions. For example, Liberal Members will conveniently ignore the fact that when they were in Government they presented legislation to privatize Teleglobe. I invite Canadians to compare their current rhetoric with their position

February 13, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
while in office as enunciated by the former Minister of National Revenue when he introduced Bill C-25, the Bill respecting the Canada Development Investment Corporation, the holding company for many Crown corporations, on May 28, 1984. At that time, the Liberal Government adopted the following position:
A second function of CDIC is to privatize... In its divestment activities, CDIC is to ensure that sales are made according to commercial standards, so that the public realizes a fair return from assets which are sold. CDIC has made initial assessments of the prospects for commercial sale of certain of the assets including consideration of market conditions and timing factors.
Despite these intentions, it was not until this Government came to power that any action was taken. Let Canadians judge the current credibility of the Official Opposition in light of its own statements.
Of course, there is always the NDP. According to the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, the NDP is, "Not necessarily against privatization. The NDP are not saying that in every case we should not privatize; we are saying you have to have sound economic reasons for it". Of course, in this case, we have sound economic reasons.

Mr. Speaker, in the light of these official positions, this Bill should rally the unanimous support of all Parties.

A privately owned, publicly regulated Teleglobe will be able to meet public policy objectives even better than a Crown corporation. Not only will we continue to enjoy first-class overseas telecommunications, but this sale will bring additional benefits to Canada through greater consumer protection, broader business opportunities for Teleglobe and the freeing up of scarce public resources to do the things that Canadians want this Government to do. I look forward to the support of the entire House in proceeding with this legislation.

The proof is that it is a corporation which has always been profitable-

The reason why I am disappointed , and I even think that the remarks of the Minister are somewhat shameful, is that the sale was made for ideological principles, not on the basis of the sound operation of a corporation, because if it were in the interest of all Canadian men and women the Government would have kept this magnificient small corporation in the public sector as a source of funds paid every year into the public treasury. No! No! It is somewhat different. I hope, because if she accused us, as Liberals, of having projects in May 1984 to privatize certain Government instruments, it is true, but we are not-

-frozen in the philosophy of Conservative thought that wants to sell at any price. One should sell when it is indicated that something is well worth selling.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: It is.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Yes, you need good economic reasons and you didn't have any. Teleglobe is a very good Crown corporation that produces well and is well administered. That is what we need. We need annual profits going into the general revenue fund of Canada from this corporation.
Teleglobe was established as the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation, the COTC, in 1950, with a legislative mandate to provide overseas telecommunications services for Canada and to participate on Canada's behalf in various international communication organizations such as the CTO, Intelsat, Inmarsat and ITU. The facilities the corporation took over were those of the Canadian international operations of Canadian Marconi Limited and Cable and Wireless Limited.
Two purposes were alluded to in the parliamentary debates on the Act which established the COTC. The first was that Canada had made a commitment during the 1945 Commonwealth Telecommunications Conference to public ownership of the providers of overseas telecommunications services. Second, it was felt that national security related overseas telecommunications facilities would be promoted by public ownership. Here, rather than promoting through public ownership, we have sold the furniture to pay for the rent.
Since 1950, international telecommunications demands have expanded enormously because of the economic growth and rapid technological developments which have resulted in higher quality and lower priced services. Teleglobe has also grown rapidly and profitably. Nevertheless, the corporation, with over $200 million in annual revenues, remains a relatively
February 13, 1987

small player in the Canadian telecommunications scene, accounting for only approximately 3 per cent of the Canadian market.
Financially the corporation gives an impression of strength and security. It has assets of $574 million and profits of over $40 million per year. The corporation has benefited from the policies of the Government which, until recently, required minimal dividends although corporate income taxes have been paid. The result has been that retained earnings have been rather large in proportion to the fixed capital stock of the company as compared to other telecommunications companies.
I would like to give an over-view of the attempts to sell Teleglobe. To date, the Government has engaged in a series of unco-ordinated initiatives and conflicting statements in its attempt to sell off Teleglobe Canada. The Government's actions with respect to this privatization can be summed up in one word, bungled. Permit me to review the Government's actions to date.
The former Industrial Expansion Minister was an early proponent of privatization. Remember his list of fire sales, Nordair, Northern Transportation Company Limited, Canada Development Corporation, de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited, Pecheries Canada Incorporated, CN route, Canadian Arsenals Limited, Canadair Limited and Nanisivik Mines Limited. The total Crown assets sold amounted to $883 million.
As I said before, we sold most of those corporations and many of them could have been profitable right where they were. While I am pleased some of them were sold, to say the least, we have to judge them case by case. I was pleased to hear the Minister say that, and that she might plan to do it that way in the future. It is too bad she did not use that yardstick in this particular instance.
Teleglobe Canada was the apple of the eye of the former Minister responsible for industrial expansion. It was a Crown corporation about which very few Canadians knew anything. It is said that in the fall of 1984 the Minister invited the former Minister of Communications and a senior official in his office to dinner. Somewhere, so the story goes, between the fish and the meat the Teleglobe sale was proposed. Immediately the official protested. There was no policy framework in which the sale could take place, he said. Without a national telecommunications policy debate, which was being planned, he said the whole bidding process was bound to get fouled up. Maybe he was thinking back to a report commissioned by the Conservatives when in opposition, although never released, which advised that Teleglobe should only be sold after a White Paper on telecommunications policy had been debated. The official must have had a crystal ball because he was certainly right. We have no national telecommunications policy and we are still in the process of meeting with our provincial counterparts to build one; co-operative federalism and national reconciliation.
Teleglobe Canada
Let us take a few moments to review what has happened in the two and a half years since that meeting. On August 1, 1985, then Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion announced that the Government was proceeding immediately with the privatization of Teleglobe. He stated that the bidding procedure put in place on that date was designed to provide all serious potential purchasers a fair opportunity to acquire Teleglobe. By letter dated September 9, 1985 Dominion Securities Pitfield, the Government's financial advisor, wrote that all bidders would be advised by October 30, 1985 whether their respective offers were acceptable and that an agreement of purchase would be signed by December 15, 1985.
In a subsequent letter dated September 11, 1985 the date for advising bidders of the acceptability of their offers was changed and they were told an agreement of purchase for Teleglobe would be signed by January 15, 1986. That was great financial management and certainly gave the businessmen a sense of confidence.
If that was not enough confusion for prospective purchasers, Dominion Securities issued a further letter dated November 12, 1985 stating, "The timetable for the sale of Teleglobe has been delayed by the temporary unavailability of the Minister responsible." As a result, they were compelled to advise that the date for the sale was being pushed back once again.
All through the spring of 1986 rumours persisted that the Government would be announcing the successful bidder for Teleglobe, but no such announcement was ever made. Then in November, 1986, almost one full year after the deal was supposed to close, what does the Government announce? It said the bidding process for Teleglobe will start all over again with new rules. Is that what the former Minister meant when he said the Government would proceed immediately with the sale of Teleglobe? Was that government policy and was it changed en route? Is that what the Minister meant when he said the bidding procedure would be fair to all parties? I suggest the Government not only changed the rules in the middle of the game but also changed the game itself.
How can we expect taxpayers to have confidence in the Government given the behaviour it has demonstrated in its management? It is no wonder that newspaper headlines in The Globe and Mail read, "Teleglobe Canada sale is act first, think later", or that The Financial Post labelled its headline, "Bidding chaos for Crowns", or most recently an Ottawa Citizen story was headed, "A privatization shambles".
The Minister alluded to the fact that the sale of Teleglobe would free up funds for other government activities. I find that rather strange in light of the fact that Teleglobe paid money to the Government every year and it certainly was not costing the Government any loss of revenue. What was the price to be paid for Teleglobe? The Government points out that the sale will result in a one-time reduction of the federal deficit. What the Government fails to indicate is that in 1985 Teleglobe wrote a cheque to the Government of Canada in the amount of $108.1 million. I call that a rather sizeable sum. I would not mind a

February 13, 1987
Tele globe Canada
cheque like that to help us move forward. Then what happened? In 1986 the company issued another cheque for $80 million. Can you tell me how that is costing the Government money? That is a very nice return to the people of Canada for the faith they had in investing in a well organized and well run public corporation. Teleglobe has been a profit generator for the Government in the past and there is every indication that that pattern would have continued in the absence of privatization.
I do not think privatization at any cost or keeping a company in the public sector at any cost is the right philosophy. We need a middle of the road, well balanced point of view which is not ideologically frozen to the left or right. That is why the Liberals were good Government and why we saw this country grow and prosper.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose for lunch, I believe I was reviewing the chronology of this divestiture. On November 19, 1986, the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) and the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) announced that the final bidding stage for Teleglobe Canada would take place. Bidders were asked once again to submit bids by January 9. On December 19, the Minister of State for Privatization tabled in the House draft legislation for the divestiture of Teleglobe. On
December 30, the Government rejected a proposal from the telecommunications companies Bell Canada, BC Tel and others, which would have allowed them to purchase 40 per cent of Teleglobe Canada.
On January 9, the last day for the receipt of bids, CDIC had seven bidders for the purchase of Teleglobe. On January 19 a story appeared in The Financial Post about the bidders for Teleglobe. Included in that list of bidders is Memotec Data Incorporated. On January 27, the CDIC board met with the various bidders and, at the conclusion of that meeting, the management of CDIC was instructed to correspond through Dominion Securities with each of the bidders to allow them to reconsider their bids.
On January 30, Mr. David Torrey of Dominion Securities sent a letter regarding the revision of bids with particular reference to by-pass, pursuant to a directive from the board of CDIC. It is interesting to note that not all the bidders changed their bids.
It should be noted that on February 2 there was no significant activity on the Toronto stock-market and some activity on the Montreal stock-market. Tuesday, February 3, was the due date for revised bids for Teleglobe Canada.
On Thursday morning, February 5, the CDIC board conducted a telephone conference call to consider the revised bids. In a memorandum to the Minister dated February 5, the board stated that it had considered all the bids for the sale. Following the conference call, it sent a very detailed letter to the Minister advising her that the bids it considered acceptable were from Caisse depot, City Financial Corporation, Gordon Investment Corporation, Intercity Gas Corporation, Memotec Data Corporation, and Power Corp. of Canada. The summary of the bidders' material was attached to the letter. The board also acknowledged that the bid from Canadian Telecom Carriers was determined to be non-compliant with the terms and conditions and their bid was conditional upon modifying three conditions of the government guidelines for the divestiture of Teleglobe Canada. Therefore, that bid was rejected.
Finally, the board suggested to the Minister that of the three highest bids received, Memotec was the first at $488.3 million. The CDIC board unanimously recommended Memotec Data as the proper company to be considered for the divestiture, or privatization, of Teleglobe. There was a halt of trading of Memotec shares on the stock-market.
A very interesting article appeared in The Toronto Star on Feburary 6. It reported the previous day's activity on the Toronto Stock Exchange and questioned why some concern had been manifest on Thursday, February 5.
Late in the afternoon of February 10, the Minister of State for Privatization informed Memotec that it was the successful bidder. All that activity on the stock exchange took place the week before the successful bidder was advised late in the afternoon on February 10.
February 13, 1987

The Minister announced at a noon hour press conference on February 11 that Memotec was the successful bidder for Teleglobe Canada. Trading in the stocks were halted for a short period of time. Philosophically I did not agree with the sale of Teleglobe, because I think it was a good and substantial company producing well with fine management, good employees and an ability to give money back to the federal coffers. Nevertheless, I did rejoice in learning that this small company had beat out some of the giants. It seemed like a very happy Cinderella story. Therefore, it was quite sad that an unfortunate cloud had now come over the head of the successful bidders.
I asked some questions in the House. At one point the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) decided not to answer my question, but answered a question outside of what I was asking. I particularly wanted to know if the Minister would conduct an immediate investigation into who in the Government, in Crown corporations or on the ministerial or departmental staff knew the name of the successful bidder and when did they know that? The Minister was as concerned, I think, as I was about this particular matter. However, what she was not able to explain was that when she knew the successful bidders, and when she knew there was some unusual activity in the stock market, why she did not stop the announcement of the sale of Teleglobe until that matter had been cleared up. I am sorry that did not take place. It would have been much better had that been done, and she could have then put her own investigation into place and this would never have become the kind of public issue which puts a cloud over this exciting moment in terms of the history of this company.
I was not happy that we have another blunder in the ongoing saga of the selling off of our Crown corporations. You must remember, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Development Investment Corporation is an agent of the Government and is part of the procedures which have to be taken into consideration as well, and it did send the very important letter to the Minister on February 5.
The Minister talked about the price to be paid for Teleglobe.
1 think I said to the Minister that because we had such a profitable company, the question of the dollars was not significant. It is a one-shot deal to wipe out a part of the deficit which the Government is well intended towards reducing. However, is that the best way to reduce it? If the Government intends to sell off its Crown jewels to reduce the deficit it will soon run out of assets. I think that is very serious. Frankly, what we are looking at seems to me to be sales which will yield short-term gain at the cost of long-term pain to our federal Treasury. Therefore, I am not particularly pleased about that and I think we are going to have to look into it a little further.
With respect to the tariffs to which the Minister alluded and the fact that she has directed, through the memorandum of sale, that there be a reduction of 13.5 per cent, it had been
Teleglobe Canada
suggested that Teleglobe's tariff was too high, and that was the prime reason for the privatization. In a brief presented to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) in August, 1986, by the Teleglobe Technical Supervisors Association, Local 1653, and the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Union, quite the contrary was revealed. The brief stated:
Our tariffs are a matter of bilateral international agreements and we must often acquiesce to the traffic structure of the overseas partners, the foreign administrations, even though Teleglobe is capable of operating profitably with lower rates.
In the case of telephone traffic, Telecom Canada receives an average of 50 cents on a dollar per conversation-minute. However, this and other problems can easily be resolved by making Teleglobe subject to CRTC regulations. Privatization is certainly not necessary to accomplish these ends.
With respect to those rates, on November 19, 1986, when the Minister of State for Privatization and the Minister of Communications announced that the Government would be proceeding with the final bidding stage in the privatization of Teleglobe Canada, it was suggested to Canadian consumers that, as a result, rates would be reduced. The Minister of State for Privatization said:
Canadian consumers and business users will benefit through reductions in overseas phone rates of at least 13 per cent on January 1, 1988, with further rate reductions likely in subsequent years. Telex charges would also fall by 10 per cent on the same date.
But this was a planned reduction. It was going to happen anyway. We did not need the privatization and divestiture for this rate reduction which will enable all Canadians to make long distance phone calls to their aunts, uncles, or friends at reduced rates. Canadians love to phone across the world because we are such an interesting mutlicultural society and come from so many areas of the world. This reduction could and would have been in place and did not require selling off this asset in order to accomplish that goal.
The Standing Committee on Communications and Culture was told when Mr. Jean-Claude Delorme, the President of Teleglobe Canada appeared before us that:
The corporation was giving consideration to a plan that consisted of a number of phases. We were considering collection rate decreases of the order of 10 per cent in 1988.
When asked whether there were further projected declines for 1988 into 1989 and 1990, the President indicated yes, but would not elaborate on what those planned reductions were. Therefore, the question of rates would have been resolved in any case.
Let us look at the monopoly status. In Bill C-38, as well as when the Minister of Communications and the Minister for Privatization announced the final round of bidding at that marvelous press conference, we were told that Teleglobe would have a monopoly staus for five years. After that date there would be no assurances that Teleglobe would continue to have such status. I must say, I am concerned about that.
When Mr. Delorme appeared before the Committee on Communications and Culture he said:
If Teleglobe is not a monopoly under the present circumstances, its viability is in serious jeopardy. By that I mean we receive our traffic and therefore our

February 13, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
revenues from two pipelines: The Telecom Canada Pipeline, which is basically the telephone pipeline, and the CN-CP pipeline, which is telex and telegraph. We do not have access to the subscribers.
Therefore, if it were to become permissible tomorrow for anyone to operate a network similar to or in competition with that of Teleglobe, then I believe the existing carriers would probably be the first candidates. And obviously, and naturally, they would seek to route their traffic via their network rather than ours. That is the reason why I say that without the protection of what we have called, in our jargon, "the single interface policy", Teleglobe's viability is in real jeopardy.
This is not me, Mr. Speaker, and it is not the Opposition who are telling the Government. This is the President of Teleglobe Canada giving a report to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, and he has serious questions. If the Government is such a good consulting mechanism, why does it not listen to the President who has had years of experience in developing a profitable company which brings very fine revenue into the coffers of this country, and recognize that without a regulated monopoly the potential for the development of this company may be seriously in jeopardy? I will examine this issue with the Minister very carefully when the Bill gets into committee. I believe this to be one of the two major flaws in the Bill, and I really regret that decision.
With respect to by-pass, because that also relates to the fact that this may not be a regulated monopoly five years down the road, if we look at November 19 of last year, when the Minister of State for Privatization reopened the bidding process for Teleglobe Canada, I indicated at that time that there did not seem to be any method by which we could prevent carriers from by-passing the Teleglobe system and by transmitting information to our neighbour to the south, the United States, and then using the American systems, which are considerably cheaper for transoceanic communication. There is the theory of the magnitude and economies of scale which come into play in terms of the American scene. The population of Canada is one-tenth the population of the United States. I think we do well, given that consideration.
The Government has taken some steps to demonstrate that carriers will not be able to by-pass the system. Under the Radio Act, the Telegraphs Act and the Railway Act the Government, we are told, will exercise its existing powers to ensure that Teleglobe remains the sole Canadian operator of facilities to provide Canada-overseas telecommunications services for a period of at least five years.
As well, under Section 64(1) of the National Transportation Act the Governor in Council is given statutory authority to vary or rescind any order or decision of the CRTC. I hope that will be enough. However, we can re-verify that when the Bill is considered in committee.
The participation of the carriers leads me to another concern, that is, the lack of participation of the telecommunications carriers in the ownership of Teleglobe. We have been told that the Memotec bid makes no provision for the domestic carriers to own a portion of Teleglobe. I find that particularly distressing as these same carriers supply 70 per cent of
Teleglobe's traffic. The November 19 guidelines for bidding provided that no more than 40 per cent of Teleglobe could be owned by telecommunications carriers. On December 29, 1986 CDIC received a bid for 40 per cent of Teleglobe from Canadian Telecom Carriers International Incorporated. It was determined to be non-compliant because it was conditional on modifying three conditions of the government guidelines for the divestiture of Teleglobe.
Having been rebuffed in their initial efforts, the telephone companies joined the bidding group that included the Caisse, other pension funds and Spar Aerospace Limited of Toronto. That bid also failed. I sincerely hope that some way will be found by the new owner, Memotec, to integrate part of the telecommunications carriers into the new Teleglobe.
My last point deals with the workers. It must be remembered that since 1979, when privatization was first advocated by the short-lived Conservative Government, all employees have been living in an atmosphere of fear and uncertainty. They operate under the continual stress of adapting to the volatile technological change that is always present in the telecommunications industries. But being asked to assume this additional stress over the last seven years can easily be perceived as indicative of the insensitivity of the present Government toward the employees of Teleglobe. I have been told that many employees have opted for early retirement, more out of fear and uncertainty than from personal desire.
Over the past year I have been in constant contact and have had the opportunity to meet and come to know many of the employees of Teleglobe whom I found to be highly organized, articulate, informed and sensitive to the important issues surrounding the privatization of a company in which many have invested their whole lifetime. I strongly believe that if it had not been for their strong voice, their futures might be less secure than they are today.
Clause 15 of Bill C-38 gives the Governor in Council, on its own or at the request of the CRTC, the power to give policy direction concerning any matters within the jurisdiction of the CRTC, and the CRTC shall give effect to the policy directives which are issued by Order in Council. I hope that these issues will be addressed in what will be an amicable way around the table as we sit down to discuss them in the legislative committee. I am looking forward to the study of Bill C-38 at which time we will examine it more closely, with particular reference to the conditions of sale and the valuation studies for the deal.
I take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of State for Privatization for her handling of the sale. I sincerely hope it will go well. It certainly has been the best of the procedures to date in terms of the divestiture of our assets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise as the NDP's privatization critic, the only male critic in this area. I mention that because the tone of the debate thus far has been so good and so positive. I hope I will not spoil it.
Since we have become so complicated in our analysis of this Bill I would like to state what the Bill is all about. We are
February 13, 1987

dealing with Bill C-38 which deals with the privatization-the selling by the Government-of a Crown corporation called Teleglobe Canada. Teleglobe has the responsibility for all overseas telecommunications entering and leaving Canada. So if one phones one's grandmother in Scotland or one's grandmother in Italy the calls must go through Teleglobe. These communications include telephone, telegraph, cable and telex communications. Teleglobe is a joint owner of submarine ocean cables and telecommunications satellite systems. Thus Teleglobe has an effective monopoly in Canada on all overseas telecommunications. In what a great Canadian, Marshall McLuhan, called the global village, overseas telecommunications are really very important. That is to say, the world has shrunk and we all live in the same village. That is why this is an important Bill.
I will not mince words. I think that the Government is selling off a crown jewel to a little known private company at a reduced price, a fire sale price. I think that the deal is bad.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is going to sell a very profitable company to a small little-known company. I did not hear ... Memotec, a small Montreal company.

That is not to say that it is a bad company, but it is a small company. It is like a minnow swallowing a whale.
The Minister anticipated my speech by saying that I wanted to maintain the status quo. In this particular case I admit that I am for the status quo. In British Columbia we have an expression which I believe was borrowed from Saskatchewan farmers. There are many retired farmers from Saskatchewan who live in British Columbia. It is 10 degrees or 12 degrees above zero in British Columbia today while it is 40 degrees below zero here with the wind-chill factor. The expression is, when something works, why fix it?
In the Minister's own words at the press conference she held the other day she said that Teleglobe had good management, that it is a well run corporation and making money. Then why sell it? In 1983 Teleglobe had profits of $53.23 million. This is money that went into the coffers of the Government of Canada. In 1984 the profits for the company were $41.17 million, while 1983 was a better year with profits of $54.6 million. This is a company which made $53 million in profits. It has good management, according to the Minister, and it is well run because of its good employees. It also has a good reputation. Why are we selling it?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Because we have a deficit.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
An Hon. Member states it is because we have a deficit. One way to pay the deficit would be to take the $50 million profits for the next few years and apply it to deficit reduction. The profits could be used in the company. Do not sell the company at a fire sale price for a short term cash
Teleglobe Canada
amount to temporarily reduce the deficit. In the long run the deficit could be reduced by keeping the company. I again ask why the Government is selling this company. The answer is that it is an ideological decision. The Government is following the trend of the Reagan administration and the Thatcher Government to privatize, sell off Crown corporations, and deregulate.
When the Government in the United States deregulated nursing homes it produced scandals in the treatment of older people. The deregulation of the airlines produced problems with respect to service for consumers. When transportation was deregulated, it was not the ordinary person who benefited, but big business interests and usually friends of people in Government. Everybody knows that this particular Government has a lot of strange friends in the business community. This decision is ideological, it is based on a theory and not on practicality.
The Minister quite rightly said that we in the NDP are not against privatization per se, but there must be a practical reason for selling a Crown corporation. For example, if there was bad management in the Crown corporation, it did not have sufficient money, or there was no public policy reason for keeping the corporation, then maybe it could be sold to the private sector. We are not being ideological about this and bianketly saying that it should not be sold, but there has to be a good reason for selling it.
I wish to give an example of what I mean by public policy. Everybody knows about Petro-Canada, the government oil company. It seems to me that when a company is out there with the big sharks, the international companies, or the oil industry, scrambling around to find energy security and supplies in a world oil crisis-we had two crises in the 1970s and we will have another one in the 1990s-there should be a window on the industry, and a government corporation in place like Petro-Canada. It would be foolish to sell off Petro-Canada and the role that it plays in the exploration of oil. For example, if we need to explore the tarsands the Government could direct that company to develop the tarsands, or Hibernia. It does not have to be done alone, it could be done in co-operation with private Canadian companies. That is a public policy purpose for having a Crown corporation.
The Government spent $886 million to buy the Gulf gas stations for Petro-Canada. I have not heard all of the arguments on this issue, so I am not coming to a firm conclusion. But one might argue that it is not a matter of public policy for the Government to own gas stations, that it may be better for small business people, community people, co-ops, or a small city. For example, in Flin Flon, Manitoba the co-ops took over gas stations. There may be no public policy argument for the Government owning gas stations. It may come as a surprise that someone from the NDP would be saying that, but it has to be looked at in that manner. In my view, there are public policy reasons for keeping Petro-Canada as an element in finding oil, and the oil plays in Canada.

February 13, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
What is the public policy argument for selling this corporation? Before I try to answer that, I wish to say that I think the onus is on the Government to show us why it is selling a company that is well managed, profitable, and which is giving good service. Another way it could be advanced is by saying that from a public policy point of view we believe that it should be in the hands of the private sector. What are some of the most important areas of life in the modern world that Canada must deal with? I would think that energy is important, and we have Petro-Canada. Transportation is important, and we have Air Canada. Communications are vital, and we have Teleglobe. Do we want the control of all of our communications to be given up to the private sector? My answer to that is no. So from a public policy point of view it should be kept in the public sector.
I wish to reiterate what I have stated. I do not think that all companies need to remain in the public sector. There could be room for privatization. The argument has to be made, and the onus is upon the Government. It has to tell us whether it is a practical reason. I do not see it here. Is there a public policy reason? I cannot see it here.
As the Minister has said, we can regulate. We will sell it to the private sector and we will regulate the company by using one of our regulatory agencies, like the National Energy Board, the Canadian Transport Commission, or the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission. In looking at the history of regulation, the problem is that the regulators have not been very strong. They tend to get in bed with the regulated. As a lawyer, I have appeared before every regulatory agency in Canada, and in my view there is not a strong regulatory system. As a matter of fact, the companies that are being regulated are pushing the regulators around, or there are weak regulators. The cable industry is a good example. So it is not good enough to say that we can regulate.
The Minister said that Crown corporations had a central role, and they have served Canada well. I ask again, why sell this corporation? I listened to the Minister's speech very carefully. It was a good speech. This Minister is a good speaker, and a good debater.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: A good Minister.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Well, we will see if she is a good Minister. The proof of the pudding will be in the eating and we will see whether she can do her job successfully. So I will suspend my judgment in that particular matter, for what it is worth.
I followed the Minister's speech very carefully, as I am sure you did, Mr. Speaker. The Minister said that Teleglobe was well managed and profitable, but it was limited. Why is it limited? She did not say why it was limited. If it is limited by law, the law can be changed. If it is limited by a mandate that has been given to it, the mandate can be changed. We should be looking at the mandate given to Crown corporations. They should be given a specific mandate, and then made accountable to Parliament and the Canadian people. But that is a reform of a Crown corporation, not a reason to sell it.
The Minister finally said it was the synergy. I notice that this was the same word that was used at the press conference the other day by Mr. Mackenzie, who is the President of Memotec, the company that is buying Teleglobe. I thought that was the key, so I asked a page to get me a dictionary. Being a traditionalist, I got it from the former Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Knowles, who is at the table today. He sent me The Oxford Illustrated Dictionary, an older dictionary. I looked up the word "synergy" in that dictionary, and it defined synergy, synergetic or synergism as co-ordination in the action of muscles, organs, or drugs. I do not know how drugs could get into the debate, so that could not have been the definition.
Then I thought, given that the Minister is a trendy person from Toronto, that it was one of these new Toronto yuppie words and that I had better get a modern dictionary. Therefore I got the Webster's Thesaurus-

speechtext: Are you filibustering?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: No. I looked at the word "synergy", and it listed: "co-acting, co-active, coefficient, conjunct, synergetic". That did not help me. Finally I went to the Webster's Dictionary.

speechtext: Do you want me to send over Winnie the Pooh for you to read?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT

I suggest that the Hon. Member should look at Webster's. I looked in it for the word "synergy" and discovered that it came from the Greek word synergos which meant working together or, broadly speaking, combined action or operation. I concluded that it was magic, that the Minister was hoping that this synergy or this magic in the private sector would somehow work. That does not make much sense. There is no reason for the Government to sell the company other than pure Conservative ideology.
The company is being sold to Memotec Data Incorporated which is a small Montreal-based data processing communications company. The Government claims to have sold the company for $608.3 million. However, when we analyse the sale carefully we find that the most Memotec will pay is $488.3 million for the company. Memotec is to pay $488.3 million to the Government for Teleglobe, and the Government is to get $102 million in accumulated cash out of the company, plus an $18 million dividend, for a total of $608.3 million. The latter payments cannot be considered part of the purchase price because they represent funds already in government hands, held by the Crown corporation.
It is also understood that as part of the $488.3 million purchasing price Memotec has said it will assume Teleglobe's debt liabilities which amount to $143 million. If this is the case, and it was not denied by the Minister in her speech- indeed, she confirmed it-the Government will only receive $345 million for Teleglobe, as no actual funds will be paid for
February 13, 1987

the debts. In other words, the company will pay $345 million and will assume the debts. That is private sector accounting, and I challenge any Tory Member to refute that. If the Government is to become involved in privatization or the private sector, let it use some of the accounting methods of the private sector.
They do not have to take money out of their pockets to pay for the debt, they just assume it. The company is in fact paying $345 million for Teleglobe. I would suggest then that the Minister start out her career as privatization Minister by telling us the truth and telling us what is the actual sale price.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has just accused the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) of not telling the truth, which is unparliamentary.
I would ask him to withdraw that totally unparliamentary remark, which is unusual for a Member of his character to use.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: If the Hon. Member said it directly, I wish he would withdraw it.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Of course I would withdraw it, Mr. Speaker, if it fell to the ears of the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) that I was in any way suggesting that the Minister of State for Privatization was trying to do this, perhaps inadvertently. I would certainly withdraw that totally, if that were the impression left.
Let me suggest that the figure is $345 million. Let me also suggest that it is a leverage buy-out, as it is called on the stock exchange. This minnow which swallowed the whale-Memotec which swallowed one of the crown jewels of the Government, the company being privatized, Teleglobe-in fact used what is called leverage buy-out. In other words, it went to the National Bank of Canada and borrowed $345 million, and then it will give it to the Government to buy Teleglobe.
How will it pay back its bank? It will use the revenues from Teleglobe, that $50 million per year. That is called a leverage buy-out. There is nothing behind Memotec. To put it more accurately, there is not that kind of money behind Memotec. It is risky business to do that, in my view. As long as the cash flows keep coming, there is no problem. However, what happens if there is a strike or some problem with telephone companies? What would happen if telephone companies suddenly found ways to reroute calls through the United States? In that event the new Teleglobe, the privatized Teleglobe, could go belly-up. The Government should not assume that particular risk. I am informed that $345 million has been confirmed by the President of Memotec and that the debt has been assumed. I think my figures are right. It is a leverage buy-out and it puts the company at risk. Quite frankly, it is a serious matter.
The Minister said that it was good for the employees.
Teleglobe Canada

Recently in this House I asked a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) concerning the employment situation at "La Cite" in Montreal-I think it was "La Cite", a cooperative housing unit in Montreal-the Government of Canada sold this building to private sector interests and two days after the sale some employees lost their jobs.

I think they were janitors and they were simply canned or laid off. How soon the Minister forgets. The case of "La Cite" is conveniently forgotten. I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) is trying to remedy the situation. I give him credit for that. He told me that he had a meeting with Louis Laberge, President of the Quebec Federation of Labour, and that he was trying to remedy the situation. It was a privatization situation, and the employees were thrown out on the street.
I have some concern that the employees in this particular case be protected. I am concerned that their pension plan be protected. Apparently it will be, but perhaps the pension plans of new employees will be different or will not be as good as the pension in the public sector. I point out that the record of the private sector in employing and dealing with women in terms of certain benefits is not as good. I ask the Minister of State for Privatization, who is also responsible in the Government for the status of women, to consider these questions in terms of privatization.
In the documents provided with the Minister's package announcing the sale no reference was made to the book value of Teleglobe. The company's book value is reported to be anywhere between $300 million and $450 million. Furthermore, its sale value is much higher, as it has an extremely good profitability picture.
When the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) was the Minister responsible for the sale of Teleglobe, British Telecom reportedly made a bid of $750 million for the company. That is a heck of a lot less than the $345 million selling price. I know the Minister of State for Privatization could say to me, "Well, would the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) want us to sell Teleglobe to a foreign country?" She is proud that Teleglobe is not going to a foreign country. But then the Minister cites, in about the next paragraph of her speech, the fact that de Havilland was sold to Boeing and it is doing great. She cannot have it both ways.
I cite this figure of $750 million to show British Telecom's projections that the company was worth a heck of a lot more than the Government sold it for. The Government, by all analysis and by all accounts, thought Teleglobe would bring in at least $600 million, and it was expected that that price would be achieved. Sadly the Government has let the company go for almost half of that $600 million. The $600 million mark also explains why the Government has tried in its press kit, and

February 13, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
press bumph, to create the impression that the company has been sold for $600 million. I said, and I will say it again, that that is not an auspicious start for a Minister who showed such great promise in the area. In my view, we should have more accurate figures.
We are completely opposed to the sale of Teleglobe because the company has been a consistent money maker. It is a monopoly and it will continue to be one. It occupies the field of communications where there is a legitimate public policy interest to be protected. It adds insult to injury to receive the paltry sum of $350 million for such a lucrative company, so valuable to the people of Canada. This is a fire-sale. Memotec is a company with reported revenues in 1985 of just under $17 million. Compare this to the revenues of Teleglobe-I am not talking about profits, I am talking about the revenues-which were $678 million in 1985. A minnow is swallowing a whale and there are some risks to it.
