Teleglobe is part of that. I am worried that the Government is privatizing part of its responsibility for international affairs. I say that seriously and I will pursue that part in committee. Teleglobe will now represent Canada on the Board of Governors. I know there are provisions in the Bill to deal with that, but this is a very strange situation with Canada giving up part of its foreign affairs in a crucial area. Australia, New Zealand, France, West Germany, Italy, Norway and Sweden all have Government controlled overseas telecommunications systems. In the United Kingdom, even the British Government, after having done a major privatization of British Telecom, has retained just slightly under 50 per cent ownership with a controlling interest. That is not the case in Canada.
Let me summarize matters, Mr. Speaker. Teleglobe has proved itself to be an effective money maker. That is undeniable, and the Minister had admitted that. It has proved itself to be among Crown corporations what one calls a crown jewel. Why sell it? Teleglobe has proved to have good management. Why sell it? It has proved itself to have given good service to Canadians. Why sell it? Other countries have either controlling interest or full ownership of international telecommunications systems. So why sell? Teleglobe has been sold for about half of what we thought it would sell for. Why sell it for half? What is the hurry? What are the real reasons for selling the company? I am looking, but I cannot find the reasons. I am not saying ideologically that we should not sell the company because it is a Crown corporation, but give me the practical and the public policy reasons. We are selling it because it is synergy-man! What is this synergy, this magical term? Will it increase the profit? What is it? Maybe some Conservatives Members will deal with it in their speeches. I would like to nail
February 13, 1987

this synergy down and find out how magical it is to convince a Government to sell a company.
The long range outlook is that the company will stay a monopoly beyond the five-year guaranteed monopoly. There is simply not a demand in Canada to have another overseas telecommunication service. The company effectively is a utility, like Ontario Hydro. Therefore, it should remain in public hands, in my view.
Despite the fact that under the sale, the Government will be able to give directives to Teleglobe for a narrow range of national security, foreign relations and international communication policy considerations, in a broader sense Teleglobe will be in a conflict between the broad policy international objectives of the Government and the profits of its shareholders, both of which are quite legitimate interests. This company will now be a hybrid and will be in a position of conflict.
There are inherent contradictions in the act of selling the company. Because it is a monopoly service, the Government does not want to sell it to the telephone companies and increase their already existent monopolies. By not selling it to the telephone companies, the company decreases its market value due to the spectre of the bypass of calls through the United States raised by the telephone companies. The upshot is that a lucrative, world-class Crown corporation is being sold for a song to a private company that will be able to maintain it as a cash cow in a guaranteed and protected monopoly environment.
What kind of business sense does the Government have? Why is it selling this corporation? I can find no public policy reason for it and I can find no practical reason for it. That is why we in the NDP will oppose this Bill.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to speak in support of the privatization of Teleglobe Canada, the latest transaction in the privatization process. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) spoke of the criteria for the sale of Crown corporations. I think those criteria were put very plainly in a document dated August 18, 1986, which stated the following:
The May Budget outlined the basic principles the Government is following to carry out its privatization initiative: to be sensitive to the concerns of management and employees in corporations considered candidates for sale; to consider the impact of privatization on consumers and market competition; to consult with provincial Governments; to avoid selling at distress prices for the sake of privatization; to follow commercial objectives when considering stages of privatization where there may be periods of mixed, private and public ownership; and to examine all related policy and financial considerations on a case-by-case basis before considering the privatization of any given corporation.
Teleglobe Canada
I think that that is very plainly and well put. As the Minister stated, the Government is proceeding on pragmatic case-bycase basis to privatize Crown corporations for which Crown ownership is no longer necessary to achieve a public policy purpose, and it is structuring these transactions in a way that maximizes future benefits for taxpayers, employees and the companies themselves.
The Opposition's tactic is to criticize these initiatives as ideological obsessions. However, Canadians know better than to believe this kind of rhetoric. The Canadians who most support privatization are those with knowledge of the performance of companies that have already been sold.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway asked over and over: "Why sell it, why sell it, why sell it?" Let us talk about why we want to sell Crown corporations and let us see what a review of past privatizations reveals.
Crown corporations that have been privatized are doing much better in the private sector than they were under government control. Benefits have accrued not only to the corporations per se but also to the management and the employees, and that was one of the Government's stated objectives. Commercial benefits can be identified because of greater freedom to compete, easier access to financial markets, and expansion of markets internationally and through joint ventures. Privatization has given these corporations the opportunity to provide better and more services to customers, to attract new customers and, in certain circumstances, to lower the cost of services.
New alliances of parent corporations and Crown corporations have enhanced technological know-how. For example, de Havilland has benefited from privatization in terms of its commercial orientation. With less bureaucratic red tape, management has become more aggressive and more private-sector oriented.
Happily, in a number of cases, the employees are the ones who are benefiting the most from privatization. Again, I would return to the question of the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway: "Why sell it, why sell it?" I know the Hon. Member is very interested in workers, and if privatization will benefit the employees, that should be a good reason to sell it.
Let us take a look at some specific cases. As Hon. Members know, the Northern Transportation Company Limited was mandated to provide reliable and comprehensive marine transportation and related services on a profit-oriented basis in the North. The Government sold this company in July of 1985 to an Inuit development corporation and it is, of course, run by the Inuit. The purchase price was $27 million. More important is what has happened since that time.
I believe it is true to say that the Northern Transportation Company Limited was well run before privatization, but it was not as aggressive as it could have been. Even though the corporation's mandate was to provide economic, reliable and comprehensive marine transportation and related services on a profit-oriented basis in northern Canada and the Arctic, the

February 13, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
Government was careful not to compete in other activities related to marine transportation in the North. Now, the new owners of the corporation see some possibility of expansion in the offshore and in eastern Arctic supply work. As they become more involved in northern development, the corporation will be able to diversify its activities. Presently, it intends to take a lead role in the north warning system.
Very often the Government will restrict the operations of a Crown corporation in order that it does not get into direct competition with other corporations in the same sector. This was true for NTCL which has now been given more freedom to compete more aggressively. The corporation is now transferring its services in the eastern Arctic area and is also entering into joint venture for the north warning system. The new flexibility given to the corporation by the privatization will serve to make it more efficient. Wider services are provided in more areas and the corporation is more able to meet local concerns. I also understand that the corporation is exceeding its own business plan. Why sell? Privatization has been good for this company, and I am sure Hon. Members are interested to know that it has been very good for the native people of the North.
What about de Havilland? Hon. Members will recall the political posturing of opposition Parties during the debate on the privatization of de Havilland to Boeing Corporation, a Seattle-based company with plants in Winnipeg and Arnprior. We have heard little since from Members of the Opposition because they do not want to bring de Havilland's success to the attention of the public.
The purchase of de Havilland Canada by Boeing has been hailed as a natural partnership by industry experts around the world. The Boeing Company has customers all over the world and more foreign customers are now looking at de Havilland products. As regional carriers become more sophisticated and solidify their links with larger airlines, the new alliance is expected to create opportunities for both companies to meet the needs of a broader base of customers in a rapidly changing and evolving market-place.
On a personal note, the regional airline on which I travel, Air Ontario, has eight Dash-8s on order. Soon I will be flying back and forth on Dash-8s. Of course their order book is so heavy we will have to wait a while for ours.
The new partnership has enhanced de Havilland's ability to compete in a highly competitive market and provided some joint venture possibilities. The company recently signed an agreement with Short Brothers PLC of Northern Ireland, a maker of small commercial planes, to explore collaboration on a new short-haul aircraft to add to their line.
These are all very good signs, of course. Yet even better news is the fact that the major beneficiaries have been the employees. The previous speaker asked, why sell? Not only do the employees have better job security but their number has
increased since the acquisition from 4,005 in January, 1986, to 5,204 in October, 1986. The privatization of de Havilland has meant jobs and more jobs in Winnipeg and Downsview. As a matter of fact, some 800 new jobs. That is why there is good reason to sell.
Let us look at the record of another company, a holding company for the fish processing corporation, Les Pecheries Cartier Inc. As Members know, that holding company was sold for $5 million to the Prudel Agrifood Corporation in April of 1986. The privatization of that company gave it greater commercial freedom by allowing it to enter into contracts with foreign enterprises. For example, a contract has been signed with Danish and English companies for the distribution of fish products. The corporation will also be expanding its marketing into the U.S. The privatization has given more freedom to the corporation and access to more and better fish markets. Pecheries Canada was able to negotiate a line of credit one week after the agreement was signed. Before privatization it had been struggling for months to increase its line of credit. With privatization it was able to lower the cost of service through cost control, particularly administrative costs. On the other hand, the company has responded better to the needs and expectations of its customers, and its employees have once again benefited a great deal. Why sell? Because it is good for the employees. They now have better job security and longer periods of work because of the greater demand in this very seasonal industry for fish products.
Those are three case studies on privatization, three very different companies handled on a very pragmatic, case-by-case basis, by this Government. They are proof that privatization means more jobs and a bright future for the employees, not to mention the taxpayer or the companies themselves. I am confident that history will repeat itself in the case of Teleglobe under the leadership of Memotec.
I would like to spend my few remaining minutes today to talk about the specific issue before this House this afternoon, the sale of Teleglobe to Memotec. Teleglobe is an important company in the Canadian telecommunications industry. Through Teleglobe our principal communication links with countries outside North America have been assured. These services are vital today and will become even more so as Canada's dependence on foreign trade continues to grow. As well, the social importance of Teleglobe cannot be ignored. The company provides the Canadian people with communication links with the rest of the world. For the many thousands of new Canadians this link with family and friends back home cannot and must not be ignored. Consequently, the Government of Canada is using this legislation, policy statements, regulatory powers, and other mechanisms to ensure the continuation of Teleglobe's vital service.
We will not allow the made-in-Canada telecommunication functions of Teleglobe to be altered or challenged. Given Teleglobe's international responsibilities this legislation will allow the Government of Canada to issue policy directives to the company within a narrow range pertaining to national

February 13, 1987
security, foreign relations and international telecommunication policy matters. Teleglobe will continue to act as a signatory to Intelsat, Inmarsat, and the Commonwealth Telecommunications Council. Our Government will retain its responsibilities and obligations as a party to these agreements. As well, the legislation subjects Teleglobe to federal regulatory authority given the vital importance of the industry to all Canadians.
The Government is committed through this legislation to ensuring that telecommunication services to all parts of Canada be provided by Canadian-owned and controlled companies as much as possible. Our Government will exercise its powers under existing legislation to ensure that Teleglobe remains for at least five years the sole authorized Canadian company in the provision of Canada-overseas telecommunications. We will ensure that Canadian domestic and international telecommunication traffic be routed through Teleglobe facilities. It is a long-standing policy of this Government that Canadian domestic and international telecommunications be carried on Canadian facilities.
As Teleglobe is a vital and viable company, Crown ownership is no longer considered necessary for the achievement of public policy purposes. The best possible terms have been found, private ownership combined with public regulation will provide significant benefit to all Canadians. Rate reductions are one of the first benefits. Overseas phone rates will fall by at least 13 per cent in January of 1988, with further reductions likely. The benefits to Teleglobe and its employees are immeasurable. The company will now have new opportunities to expand and grow through an ability to pursue new business opportunities. Given the history of past privatization efforts by this Government we have every reason to expect that many new jobs will be the result of this sale. Additionally, tax dollars used for Teleglobe will now be freed up for other priority initiatives of our Government.
In the bidding process a number of restrictions were put on interested companies. First, provision was put into place to ensure effective Canadian control at all times. Total nonresident ownership is restricted to 20 per cent. As well, to restrict domestic telephone companies from gaining control of Teleglobe they are restricted to acquiring a maximum of 40 per cent of the company initially. It was essential that some company shares be made available to employees through a share purchase plan. As well, after a period of adjustment for the new owners, the Government will take steps to ensure that some shares in the company will be sold publicly. It is nice that the employees can participate in this very successful company and own a piece of it. That is another reason that it is so very good for employees. As well, any successful bidders had to ensure that employee concerns would be addressed. Memotec has met and in some cases exceed the Government's expectations with respect to the future of the employees.
Memotec has agreed that the headquarters of Teleglobe will remain in Montreal, and it has agreed to continue existing collective agreements. It has agreed not only to provide pension coverage which meets existing industry standards for
Teleglobe Canada
new employees, but to continue coverage for existing employees in a plan equivalent to what they now enjoy as federal government employees. In addition, the employee share purchase plan to which Memotec has agreed exceeds our requirements. The company is offering employees a 5 per cent share in the company at 90 per cent of the relevant purchase price with a five-year interest-free loan. What more could be asked to ensure the security of these employees?
The Government has made every possible effort to ensure that the sale of Teleglobe does not interfere with the national telecommunication network which our Government realizes is of such importance to all Canadians. Teleglobe cannot cease business or amalgamate without the approval of the House. CRTC approval is necessary for transfers of effective control or the disposition of substantive amounts of assets of this company. If Teleglobe contravenes these conditions, the CRTC has the authority to force the disposition of the offending shares.
Along the same lines, the Government has taken special care to ensure that telephone communication companies will never be in a position to control Teleglobe.
Since they are compatible industries, it is obvious that telecommunication companies of Canada must be represented on the board of directors of Teleglobe. This legislation guarantees them a continued representation proportionate to their holdings, but is limited to a maximum of one-third of the total membership of the board. Additionally, as a further precaution, officers of Teleglobe cannot be officers of either the telecommunication companies or their affiliates.
Please do not get the idea that Teleglobe will have its hands so badly tied that it cannot move. The Government has set down minimum requirements. These requirements are essential if they are to ensure that all Canadians have access to the same levels of service they are currently enjoying. Beyond these, Teleglobe is free to enlarge, expand, and grow as its own business interests dictate.
Clearly the sale of Teleglobe is a good deal. These are enormous benefits. This sale will provide enormous benefits to everyone.

Teleglobe Canada

Mr. Speaker, I join in this debate on the matter of the privatization principle itself and, of course, the specifics of the sale of Teleglobe which is proposed and is up before Parliament for approval, and the bargain basement rates which have been permitted in this sell-out of a very important Crown corporation. I would like to quote the Communications and Electrical Workers of Canada as they look at this issue. It has an Ottawa by-line:
For sale: One world class telecommunications company. Provides a vital Canadian presence in international communications. An impressive track record of efficiency and productivity. Consistently one of the most profitable corporations in the country.
Must sell quickly as present owner getting out of business. Will sell to highest bidder. No preconditions. Contact Mulroney and Company, House of Commons, Ottawa.
This is not quite the advertisement the Minister put in the newspapers, but I think it is very much the sense of the approach of the Government to the sale of Teleglobe. If we look at the concerns of the employees, the people who have made this a very profitable company, we find that in this case the Communications Workers of Canada have urged that any privatization decision be put on hold until the completion of the former Minister of Communications announced review of the national telecommunication policy. The suggestion is, and I think it is very reasonable, that the privatization of a particular company in the telecommunication field should not be looked at alone, but should be looked at in the context of a national policy on telecommunications, a national policy which we do not have at present, and is a question of some speculation.
Teleglobe Canada

Teleglobe Canada is a Crown corporation whose responsibility is to ensure the transmission of international telecommunications in Canada. These telecommunications are made mostly through telephone, cable distribution, and telex transmissions. Teleglobe is active co-owner of intercontinental submarine cables and satellite communications systems. Throughout this country, overseas telephone calls account for 85 per cent of its revenues.
Teleglobe Canada had demonstrated its obvious profitability. Why should we sell such a Crown jewel? That is the question which a good many Canadian men and women are asking.
In the long run Teleglobe will probably remain a monopoly beyond the five years it will be guaranteed. The demand in this area of overseas telecommunications is simply non-existent. This company is not just a profitable concern but it should remain part of the public sector.
Although the Government will provide directives for tightening national security in connection with external relations and for international telecommunications policies, Teleglobe Canada will to a considerable extent be in a conflict between policy-dictated objectives on the one hand and the normal considerations of a business that is supposed to make a profit, on the other. That is the case at Intelsat.
There are some very definite contradictions, down to the actual conditions of sale. Just because this is a public service that has a monopoly in its field, the Government did not want to sell to another telephone company, claiming that this would further enhance an existing monopoly. However, not selling to another telephone company means the market value of the company drops, owing to fear that the company's further development could be delayed. This puts downward pressure on the sale price. In the final instance, a profitable Crown corporation with an international reputation has been sold for a song to a private company that can use it as a source of funds to protect it against other monopolies on the market. What kind of deal does the Government think it is making?

Teleglobe has always been a money-maker. Its profit has improved considerably over the years. With respect to its profits, its net income after taxes in 1985 was $53.2 million. In 1984 the company's profit was $41 million-plus. In 1983 the profit figure was $54.6 million. In 1982 it was $47 million. In 1981 it was $36 million. In 1980 it was $35.9 million. In 1979 it was nearly $20 million. In 1978 it was $14.5 million. In 1977 it was $14.9 million. In 1976 it was $12 million, and in 1975 it was $11 million. The company has had consistent and sizeable profits over the years. In recent years its profits have been substantial when one takes into consideration the size of the company. It is known as the jewel of Crown corporations.

February 13, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
In their original approach to privatization the Conservatives' idea was to make a package of companies, including some that they wanted to get rid of because they were not doing well. To sweeten the package the idea was to include Teleglobe because it is such an attractive company. That was the first reason for putting Teleglobe on the block. We have now gone by that point. The other companies have not been sold, or they will be sold separately. In this case Teleglobe has been put on the block by itself.
The Government wishes to sell Teleglobe to Memotec Data, a small Montreal-based data processing and data communication company. The Government claims that the sale price is $608.3 million. Estimates of the company's worth are certainly around that amount. Given its continued profitability some people might think it is worth even more. However, no one is suggesting that anyone is paying too much by having to pay that amount of money for the company. The figure of $608 million is an exaggeration. It makes the price look a lot better than it is in fact. When one looks at the terms of the sale more carefully the total begins to diminish. It goes down to a considerably more modest sum.
Memotec is to pay $488.3 million to the Government for Teleglobe. The Government will receive $102 million of accumulated cash from the company, plus $18 million in dividends. That is what brings the total up to $608.3 million in total. However, the figures with respect to the dividend and the money in the accumulated cash account are not really part of the purchase price since this is money which the Government already has. It is money already in the hands of Teleglobe. This is a sort of a buying-out of oneself. It is not a genuine transfer of money from a private company to the Government. It is not looking after the interests of taxpayers by getting a good price for this jewel of Crown corporations.
As part of the $408.3 million purchase price Memotec has said that it will assume Teleglobe's debt liabilities which amount to $143 million. If this is the case then the Government will only be receiving $345 million for Teleglobe, since no actual funds will be paid for the debt. Memotec has said that it plans to raise $345 million through a loan. It will borrow $225 million from the National Bank and raise the additional $125 million through an issue of debentures to institutional investors. This is a situation of a very small company buying a much larger company with not very much money. It is borrowing some of the money and getting the rest out of the accumulated funds of the company. It is not in any sense an infusion of new money from the private sector to purchase and pay a fair amount of money for this going concern.
In the press the sale of Teleglobe has been described as a minnow swallowing a whale. It is remarkable how this very small company should be able to proceed in this fashion. We are all concerned with some of the irregularities that appear to have occurred in terms of the share trading in this stock. There
are too many coincidences with respect to the value shooting up very quickly. That has to be a matter of concern as well.
One improvement the Government has made as a result of a criticism of the Bill and its original intentions in selling Teleglobe has been to give better protection to the employees of the company. They have been very clear. Several of their unions have made strong representations with respect to protection of the employees, especially with regard to pension funds.
The employees of Teleglobe have had the benefit of Public Service pensions. It is a good pension plan. The Government's initial position was that the employees of the new corporation would have to accept what the going pension benefit package was in that industry, whereas in fact they had a superior one. I am glad to see that the Government has agreed to ensure that existing employees at least will continue with the superior benefits which they have. Pensions are certainly important for people. We would like to see people have better pension plans, not reduced pension entitlements, especially for those who have fought for them and who have obviously given up collective bargaining to get good pensions. We would rather see more people getting good pensions than fewer. Unfortunately, this will not hold for any new employees of the company. We will have the very unhappy situation of a two-tiered system in which new employees will not be treated as well as previous employees of the company.
The Government has also said it will be introducing legislation to prevent the possibility of telephone companies bypassing Teleglobe and routing overseas telephone calls through the United States overseas telephone systems, which is a deregulated system and one with a larger market. This is important because one of the reasons Teleglobe is reported to have been sold for such a modest price is the alleged threat of bypass by the Canadian telephone companies. If a bypass is permitted then consumers will take advantage of the lower prices through the United States and the company would certainly not survive either in public hands or in private hands. It would not be able to survive that very substantial competition.
So we have a situation in which the company's survival, whether in public hands or private hands, depends on this type of protection. In effect, it has to be a monopoly. It has been guaranteed monopoly status for five years. It seems likely that it will continue as a monopoly after that. The point is that right now it is a monopoly. If it is to continue as a monopoly then it should be treated as one, as a utility. There is a public interest in regulating it very carefully. I suggest that there is a public interest in owning it as a utility which provides a service needed by everyone. It is a service in which the Government has a particular concern in seeing it well handled. I note that other countries have maintained public companies in this domain. There are security reasons for having a single company under public control. This ensures the protection of this extremely important telecommunication link.

February 13, 1987



Teleglobe is a profitable Crown corporation in an industry that must be regulated by the Government, even after privatization. In other countries, the same service is provided by public corporations. Privatization of Teleglobe is not necessary, useful or sensible.
I also would like to raise some questions about the treatment of employees. The Government has met the demands of employees now working for the corporation, but it has not responded to the demand for justice for all employees with respect to pensions.
Mr. Speaker, I think my twenty minutes are up.
Before concluding, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-38, An Act respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time this day three months hence."

speechtext:
Telecommunications is a very important industry. Overseas telephone calls are an important part of life. Our population uses the telephone more than any other population in the world, and telephones are used substantially for overseas communications. Canada has a large number of immigrants who wish to keep in touch with their families. Our telephone patterns are rather different from American patterns where more of the international communications are for business reasons, and rather less for family and social purposes. The pattern in Canada is an enormous amount of use of international telecommunications for keeping families and communities in touch. That pattern is a rather distinctive one, and people want high quality services.
Some countries have gone the deregulation route. For example, Britain has sold its international telecommunication company, however it did maintain a 49 per cent public share. Of course, countries which have permitted private operation are highly regulated. That has been the pattern. If we proceed with this, there would still be a great deal of regulation. So the situation is neither fish nor fowl. If it is a private company, it will have the advantages of a monopoly and those of making a lot of money, yet there will still have to be that protection. It seems it is a little bit unfair that way. A previous Conservative Member talked about the market and conservatism and competition. There is no competition where there is a monopoly. The only manner in which we could have competition is if the calls were placed through the United States. If that happens, the company would fold completely.
So there is a protected market in order for the company to survive, whether it is public or private, yet the company reaps all the benefits of this monopoly without facing real competition. It is protected in this fashion. It seems to me that it is quite fraudulent and hypocritical to talk about conservatism and promoting enterprise. That will not happen, it will continue to be protected. This is phoney politics in trying to protect the virtues of the small entrepreneur out there competing. That will not happen. Telecommunications is a different type of industry, and it is futile to use that model.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) for introducing his motion which, as Your Honour pointed out, will require a constitutional amendment. The proposal is that Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights be amended as follows:
Everyone including a human foetus or unborn human being has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
That is the form of the resolution. I know that some Hon. Members in the House have mentioned that a constitutional amendment is always very difficult, and I would agree with that. However, at the same time I would have to say that that misses the point; that is not the reason the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe brought forward the resolution.
If the Hon. Member could get what he wants, that is the protection in our laws of the rights of unborn children, I know he would accept an amendment to the Criminal Code. I think that is beside the point. I think we are here to talk about the principle of the rights of unborn children, to which I would like to address myself.
I hope my own position on the subject has been made very clear. I tried to make it very clear to my constituents in Niagara Falls during the 1984 election campaign. Everything I have done and have said I have tried to make consistent with that. Early in January I was an open line show and someone asked for my opinion on the subject of abortion. I indicated to him, just as I had in the summer of 1984, that I was very clearly opposed to abortion and that I would support resolutions in the House of Commons which helped protect the rights of unborn children.
He asked me on the radio: "Didn't you see that poll which came out recently indicating that most people are in favour of abortions?" I made two points to him which I should like to
February 13, 1987

repeat in the House. I think polls in this area can be very misleading. It depends upon how the question is formulated. The result depends upon the way in which the question is asked. If the wording of the question is changed, the result is different. I do not believe and have never believed that important moral questions affecting the country should be decided on the basis of public opinion polls. As well I indicated to him that it was a deep moral conviction of mine and that it was not something I would likely change very easily.
I read with interest the debate which preceded my speaking on the motion. I noted the very eloquent speech on this particular subject by the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). At one point he indicated to the mover of the motion that probably there would not be a foundation for his view in the Bible, that he would not find it in the teachings there. I am very reluctant to challenge an ordained clergyman on what the Bible says or does not say, but I remember a passage which I heard read out loud in church which I have always thought was very significant.
In preparing to speak to the motion, I decided to try to find it. It is from The Book of Jeremiah. Chapter 1, verse 4, begins as follows:
Now the word of the Lord came to me saying,
"Before I formed you in the womb I knew you,
And before you were born I consecrated you-"
I always thought those words were very significant. I was a teenager the first time I heard them spoken. I thought it very significant that the Bible did not say: "I knew you after you came out of the womb and I consecrated you just at the moment you were born". It seemed to me to be very clear. 1 believe it is a passage which should be of interest to Hon. Members.
The question of abortion is settled in my own mind for a number of reasons. I suppose all of us bring our upbringing and our experiences of life to our consideration of every moral question. I do that, and one of the reasons I am against abortion is that so often I find the arguments in favour of abortion to be so unsatisfactory.
One argument put forward by those who oppose stricter laws in the area of abortion is that the child should only acquire rights after it is viable outside the womb. With that line of reasoning then it is incumbent upon legislators to determine at what point a child can survive outside the womb. In different jurisdictions we see different determinations of just when that is, whether it is 27 weeks, 24 weeks, or 18 weeks. However, the point I should like to make is that advances in technology make that sort of consideration irrelevant.
We have seen cases again and again where children can survive outside the womb, which point us in the direction that surely human life begins at the moment of conception. That is where medical technology is leading us.
I am struck as well by stories which happen occasionally. 1 remember one, perhaps six years or seven years ago, about a
Right to Life
young woman who was in the hospital for an abortion. All the papers had been signed and sealed, and there was to be an abortion. They took out the child and the child was alive; the child cried. Talk about a moral dilemma! Is that child which just screamed immediately imbued with all the rights and privileges Canadian citizens have taken centuries to acquire, or is it something that can be put in the ashcan? There was a moral dilemma in that hospital operating room. It was resolved in favour of giving life support systems to the child, and the child subsequently died. However, it points out again that surely human life must begin at the moment of conception.
One argument used by individuals in favour of abortion is that they characterize people like myself as not compassionate or not caring. I remember being on the Student Council of Queen's University around 1973. There was a debate about whether the Council should be giving money to an agency which included in its services an abortion referral service. I became involved in an argument with one of the other members. He pointed out the classic case. He said: "What about the woman who has 11 children and finds that she is pregnant again, and her husband is going to beat her if she has any more children? What about her?" I say that my heart goes out to that individual. I am compassionate and caring when I am told that a single, 17 year old girl in Grade 11 finds herself pregnant. That is a tragedy. Both cases are tragedies. However, I say: "Don't compound the tragedy".
One of the arguments I do not buy is the one used by those in favour of abortions, namely, "we want to make sure every child in Canada is a wanted child". That is the biggest joke in the whole issue. Every child born in Canada is a wanted child, if not by its natural parents then by the tens of thousands of Canadians who want to adopt children. I cannot tell you how many times I have been in my law office with young couples who have told me of their difficulties in adopting children. People in tears have told me there is nothing they wanted more than to adopt a child but they could not do so because of the abortion laws. To those who do not want children in Canada I say that there are tens of thousands who do. Why not turn an unfortunate situation into someone else's joy?
Let me say that I am pleased to be associated with the cause of the unborn. It has always been my belief that the more helpless the individual is in society the more likely that his or her rights will be trampled upon and ignored. It is all the more incumbent upon those who are elected to public office to make sure that those rights are not trampled upon and not forgotten.
Some day when our grandchildren or our great-grandchildren read these debates maybe this whole problem will be resolved. It may be that those who flaunt the abortion laws, or those who open up abortion clinics, the Henry Morgentalers of this world, will be the modern day saints of this era. Maybe. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think so. I do not buy the arguments of those who ask us to relax the laws. I do not believe the laws are tough enough. That is why I support the motion of
3438

February 13, 1987
Right to Life
the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe, and regardless of how society will some day conclude this issue, I want to say that I am pleased to stand up for the rights of unborn children. It is what I believe and why I am so proud to support this motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Grey- Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) for placing this important issue of the rights of the unborn before the House of Commons of Canada. I want the Member and the House to know that hundreds of my constituents in Langley, Surrey and Aldergrove have expressed their support for his motion through letters, petitions and telephone calls. I know the debate has raged for many years and has been the source of bitter controversy and division among Canadians, but there is no doubt in my mind that people on all sides of the debate speak from sincere and heart-felt convictions.
Normally when people in debate reach an impasse, we are prepared to agree to disagree and to see if some kind of a workable compromise can be attained with which both sides could live. It is unfortunate but inevitable that in the debate on abortion, compromise is all but impossible. For this debate involves quite literally a matter of life and death. A young life is either snuffed out or allowed to develop. There is no in between or compromise position.
I use the term "young human life" deliberately because that is in the amendment and it is most appropriate. It is unfortunate that so much of the abortion debate has come to focus on terminology. There are those who refer to unborn humans as foetus just to avoid using the term human being, which they feel is inappropriate when applied to a six or 10 week-old child in his or her mother's womb. But whether we use the term foetus or unborn baby, there is no doubt that what we are speaking of is human life, of this there can be no doubt.
I am not interested in getting involved in a numbers game. How many words have been spoken and written regarding the point at which a developing life can be called a human being? Is it six hours or six days? Some say six weeks, others say 16. Others claim that not until the baby is outside the womb can it be called a human being. All have their graphs, charts and doctors' statements to justify their view as though doctors could not disagree as strongly as anyone else on the issue. This is not a medical issue, it is an issue of moral, ethic and cultural values.
The creation of life remains one of the most profound mysteries of this world. Scientists have become better at describing that process and in rudimentary forms science can reproduce it. I have great respect for science, and I am not inclined to belittle the kind of knowledge that it yields, but for all its ability to address the "how" questions, it cannot give us the answers to the "why" questions. Science is no more qualified to pronounce judgment on the value of human life and whether or not it should be compromised than is any field of endeavour.
As my colleague from Grey-Simcoe pointed out in earlier debate, those of us who oppose abortion run the risk of perhaps being labelled as insensitive, as uncaring in regard to the heartbreaking circumstances from which all too often abortions follow. Nothing could be further from the truth, and it is not easy for me to advocate a position which I am aware could make heavier the burden being carried by people who are already heavily burdened.
The prospect of an impoverished unemployed single young woman having to cope with an unwanted pregnancy is terrible and difficult to contemplate. Suffering and misery are things much more easily considered in the abstract than faced as part of daily life and it is likely true that only those who have known it first hand can really understand it. Despite this, it seems to me to be absolutely essential to distinguish between an unwanted pregnancy on the one hand and an unwanted child on the other. At a time when childless couples yearn to share their homes and their love through adoption, I do not believe there is such a thing as an unwanted child. What is unwanted is the fear, the social stigma, the guilt, the economic burden, or just the plain inconvenience that can motivate a mother to terminate the life she is carrying. To this extent the abortion epidemic has its roots in the attitudes and values of society and the often overwhelming pressures they can place on the individual, for which we must all share responsibility.
While the values of our times will determine the course of a new human life, for better or for worse, the changing values of society have no bearing on the intrinsic value of life itself. Once that life is there, it is a fact as real as anything else in the world, and from that moment on at least two human lives are vitally affected by the course which it runs, that of the mother and that of the human infant now developing.
How often we have heard that abortion is a matter between a woman and her doctor, or that it is a medical matter only? These assertions, which are often put forward as though they were arguments merely beg the question. They pre-suppose that the infant human human life is of no intrinsic value and unworthy of consideration. This is precisely the point, however, on which the entire debate turns.
From the moment of conception to the moment of death, life is a seamless development guided by numerous factors ranging from genetic information to the vast multitude of experiences that comprise a lifetime. Whether human life is two weeks, two months or two years old, the spark of life that burns within that infant-that life-giving impulse-is as real, as precious, as miraculous and as sacred as the life within any of us here today.
After witnessing the horrors of this century which has seen so much life destroyed through war, famine and numerous atrocities that Governments and individuals have inflicted upon their fellow human beings, have we not learned that the deliberate termination of innocent life is not just a criminal offence, a contravention of laws? Have we not learned that it is
February 13, 1987

an affront to something even greater, that sacred dimension of life in which human dignity in its most profound sense originates? When all is said and done, we still find ourselves speaking of human life. Whether we approach the question from a religious or a secular perspective, have we not yet learned that it is the most precious of all things?
Our modern-day social consciousness is preoccupied with human rights. We set up commissions and investigative committees, we pass laws and regulations, we create watch-dog agencies to ensure that that these rights are respected. We are rightly concerned with safeguarding the quality and dignity of human life, but our consciousness of the sacred dimension of human life seems to have somehow dissipated. For me, this represents an impoverishment of the human spirit. Although I fully support the motion of my colleague to have the rights of the unborn enshrined in our Constitution-Mr. Speaker, I see you signalling that my time is just about up.
In conclusion, let me say that sitting in the gallery today is my 10 year old son Kraig. On the way here, I said to him: "I'm going to speak about abortion today. What do you think?"
He said: "Well, I think all kids should have the right to live".
I agree with my son's statement. When my son was in his mother's womb, the doctor told us that we may have to consider an abortion. He asked how we felt about that. We said that we must give this child a chance to live. We gave this child a chance to live and we love him. Abortion is not right.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am also glad to have an opportunity to speak to this resolution.
I think it is important that we hear all sides of this extremely important and very emotional subject. I respect very much the views of my colleagues, even though my own may be different.
We are speaking, of course, on Motion No. 37 to amend the Constitution Act, Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights, so that it reads as follows:
Everyone ncluding a human foetus or unborn being has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
This is a very emotional subject and a very personal one. We have very personal and in some cases very religious views on it and I think it is extremely important that we respect the views of others. That is why I believe very much in choice. I think it is important that people make their own decisions on this matter and that we not impose our views on others.
It is clear that the real intent of this proposed amendment is to restrict access to abortions. I am sure the mover of the motion would agree with that. The Hon. Member wants to reverse Canadian Government policy which allows abortion under the Criminal Code when approved by a recognized therapeutic abortion committee of a hospital. The Hon. Member's views on this matter and the views of other Hon. Members go against the views of the majority of Canadians, but that is his right and the right of my colleagues who support
Right to Life
his stand. Indeed, during testimony before the Private Members' Business Committee, the Hon. Member who sponsored this motion said that the only circumstances in which a woman should have access to abortion is if it could be proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the death of the mother would result if the procedure were not performed.
Before talking about restricting access to abortions, I believe we should talk about guaranteeing equal access to abortion services to which women are legally entitled under the current law. There are serious discrepancies in access to abortion services across Canada. Not all eligible hospitals have established therapeutic abortion committees and in those that have, the policy varies very much from one to the next. In 1984, of the 244 hospitals with therapeutic abortion committees, 18 did not perform any abortions while another 24 performed very few. As of June 1986, women in Prince Edward Island had no access to services in their province because the only remaining therapeutic abortion committee was dismantled. During the summer of 1986, abortion services in Newfoundland were temporarily unavailable because the only doctor on the Island willing to perform the procedure was on extended sick leave. In Alberta, women must travel long distances to obtain services.
The burden of unequal access to services to which women are legally entitled falls most heavily on rural, low-income women and on poor women who cannot afford to travel and simply do not have equal access. Unequal access means that women must resort to back room abortionists. That is what would happen if this resolution were to go through. I must say that it would not stop abortions, and stopping abortions is obviously the desire and intent of the people who support it. Abortions will continue to occur. That is the reality. However, these abortions would be illegal, back room, dangerous ones which would put the health of women at risk.
Unequal access makes a mockery of equality guarantees enshrined in our Charter of Rights. To further restrict access to abortions by amending the Constitution is, I believe, not the way to achieve what we all want, and I do think we all want to eliminate the need for abortions. Surely this should be our goal.
The prevention of unwanted pregnancies is certainly preferable to abortion. I believe we all agree with that. I would like to state right here that being pro-choice does not mean that one is in favour of abortion. This seems to be interpreted as a pro or anti-abortion issue, and that is not the case at all. I do not know of anyone who is really in favour of abortions. However, being pro-choice does mean that one respects another person's right to make her own decision based on her own circumstances.
I want to stress the point that we must get to work on prevention. Those who feel that there must be a restriction of access to abortion should be the first to work on prevention. If this resolution went through, it would not stop abortions. That is a fact of life. The only thing that will stop abortions is prevention.

February 13, 1987
Right to Life
Prevention requires birth-control education in schools. The whole scare over AIDS is finally beginning to make many people aware that we need a very positive family-life education program including birth-control information in the schools. We must teach young people to make responsible choices about sexual relationships. We must talk with them openly so that they are aware of the full implications of their decisions and behaviour.
Prevention means increasing funding for groups like Planned Parenthood that promote awareness about birth control and family planning. More effective prevention requires more research into reliable, safe birth-control methods. I was told the other day by an authority that the increase in abortions directly correlates with the failure in birth-control methods. The Government has cut back on research in that area, and that is one area in which funding should be increased. Those who support this resolution should agree with that. Prevention, education and research can reduce the need for abortion. Recent studies, such as those done by Planned Parenthood in Ontario, have demonstrated that public education reduces the unwanted pregnancy rate, particularly in teenagers. We have a very high incidence of adolescent pregnancies, which is a very deplorable trend. Education reduces the number of abortions and does not increase sexual irresponsibility. That is what the study shows.
We talk about prevention but we seem to talk about this question only as it relates to women. Surely men have an equal if not greater obligation to prevent unwanted pregnancies. I wish that were stressed much more.
In cases where unwanted pregnancy does occur we must make sure women have access to safe abortions, if that is the decision. We do not want to impose our decision on anyone. I do not anyway. Surely no Member wants to force desperate women to seek back room abortions with non-medical butchers. It is the basic right of any woman to make the decision about maternity. A decision to have an abortion should be a matter between a woman and her physician. This is not only the position of the NDP; it is the position espoused by the Canadian Medical Association way back in 1971. The CMA also agrees there may be justification for abortions on non-medical, socio-economic grounds. Many feel that the UN definition of health should be used in present laws.
We want to ensure that all children enter this world under the best possible circumstances, wanted and loved and cared for with adequate resources. We want to ensure adequate support services to families before and after they make a choice to have children. These support services must include affordable, accessible and quality child care. Support services must help to relieve the stresses on families which lead to their breakup. Lack of adequate income is a major cause of family stress today and certainly is a major factor in the reason that some women consider abortions. Support services must be geared to the new realities of Canadian families. In many cases
both parents work, many families are headed by single parents, and more egalitarian reglationships exist between parents with respect to their parental duties. Let us work on sensible solutions to strengthen families and enable people to make responsible choices about having and caring for children.
It is true that this motion recommends that the Government consider the advisability of amending the Constitution Act. We are therefore not debating an amendment to the Constitution per se. Nevertheless, I think even those who would restrict access to abortion may wonder whether a constitutional amendment of this kind is an appropriate way to proceed. As a Private Members' Motion this proposal will receive a maximum of only five hours of debate. This is a precedent for other constitutional amendments, let us remember. Is this the amount of time we want to devote to such a motion? As it is currently worded, it would not be referred to a parliamentary committee for further study. There would be no opportunity for interested Canadians to be heard on this issue. We know many Canadians feel passionately about the issues we are discussing. Surely they should be heard on this issue.
The Hon. Member who sponsored the motion must also be aware that amending the Constitution is no easy task. Amending Section 7 would require resolution of the legislative assemblies of two-thirds of the provinces representing in the aggregate 50 per cent of the population of Canada. It is clear that regardless of what subject is being considered, if this House is going to recommend that the Government consider an amendment to the Constitution, the supreme laws of our country, five hours of debate during Private Members' Hour is not the way to proceed. Even those who support the intent of the motion must surely have problems with that and also with the wording of the proposal. I hope for that reason alone that they will vote against the motion.
Changing the wording of Section 7 of the Charter has serious implications for legislation already in place and the case law built up around that legislation. For example, the Criminal Code clearly differentiates between a human being and an unborn child. The Code states that a child becomes a human being when it has completely proceeded from the body of its mother. The law has therefore until now selected birth as the point at which the foetus becomes a person with full and independent rights. Changing the wording of the section also has serious implications for other sections of the Charter, other human rights legislation, indeed all legislation which uses the word "everyone". It is clear that amending Section 7 has serious implications for the whole legal framework already in place. For that reason alone, regardless of the position on the substantive issue here, I would hope that my friends will join my colleagues and me in the NDP in voting against this motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity of adding a few words in the debate on the motion before us today. I want to commend the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) for the motion he has put
February 13, 1987

forward. It is a very important motion and I agree with its thrust.
The motion would amend Section 7 of the Charter of Rights by defining the word "everyone" in that section. It would include a human foetus or unborn human in the word "everyone" or "person", and therefore having the right to life, liberty and security of person, and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. It is important that we know exactly who is included when we refer to "everyone" or to a "person". At present there is quite a bit of debate about this subject and our practice now with regard to abortion suggests that an unborn human being or foetus is not a person because we deprive that foetus of the right to life through the procedure of an abortion.
In concluding her remarks the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said that this is a very important issue and therefore should not receive just five hours of debate. The Hon. Member should perhaps contact the Standing Committee on Private Members' Business, of which I am a member. She would find that this motion has been designated as a votable motion. It will receive up to five hours of debate and then there will be a mandatory vote. That is a new feature in Private Members' Business. Motions or Bills can be designated as votable, as this one today is. If the motion is adopted by the House, it would go to the appropriate committee. It would be studied and then referred back to the House for a further two hours of debate and another vote. To suggest that all we are doing on a very important topic like this is debating it for five hours is incomplete. There is more to come should the House approve the motion.
When the Special Joint Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate was studying the Charter of Rights and amendments to the Constitution in 1981, Mr. Robert Keller-man, legal counsel to CARAL, appeared before the committee and said that in his opinion the majority of Canadians do not believe the foetus to be a human person or included in the word "everyone" as suggested in this motion. Further, he drew attention to the fact that according to his view of the Criminal Code, the foetus only becomes a person once it is independent of its mother; in other words, either prematurely or at the term of the pregnancy when the foetus emerges from the mother's womb and is independent of the mother.
Mr. Kellerman's comments bring us to the fundamental question at hand in this matter. Is the unborn a potential human being, or a human being with potential? Contrary to Mr. Kellerman's view, it is my contention that the foetus is, from conception, a human being with potential.
My comments and consideration of this motion will involve three aspects: medical, legal and social.
I am not a doctor, but I think all of us are capable of learning from what the medical profession can teach us. One
Right to Life
fact is that all of the information necessary for the development of each of us as a unique human being is contained in the genetic code that is present in us from the moment of conception. Nothing more ever need be added because the uniqueness of each of us-the colour of our eyes, our size and our various abilities-has already been established at that moment. This is a consideration we must take into account from the beginning.
Let us consider the foetus as a medical patient. As a result of medical treatment of the foetus itself, it is now considered as a patient for treatment. You do not look upon a foetus as a piece of the tonsil that is removed and discarded. It is now possible through operations, such as blood transfusions or corrective surgery while the foetus is still in the womb, to treat the foetus as a unique individual. In fact, medical technology has come to the point where the foetus can be removed from the womb, operated upon, and replaced so it may come to its full term.
It is remarkable that developments of neo-natal technology now allow for the viability of a foetus as early as five months after conception. This is forcing the reconsideration of Canadian legislation as well as American legislation.
American legislation on abortion is based upon a trimester system. In the First trimester, the state has really no interest in the foetus as a human being, but simply treats it as tissue. In the second trimester, the mother's health is a major consideration. In the third trimester the state takes on an interest in the well-being of the foetus due to the argument of viability, that it could now exist on its own outside the womb as a premature child with care in a hospital.
According to Canadian abortion law, it is possible, although not likely, to have an abortion from the time the mother knows she is pregnant and wishes to have the abortion until just before birth itself. Surely we must re-evaluate that, because it is totally unacceptable.
Let us consider what other countries have done. In West Germany in 1975, the Lower Court asked the Upper House and the Supreme Court to look into the question of when a foetus begins the civil right to life. The German Supreme Court was well aware of what Germany had done between 1933 and 1945, when it denied civil rights to certain groups within its society. The court wanted to take special care in responding to this question, to make sure it looked at it carefully. It called together a group of 133 scientists, geneticists, gynaecologists and others from around the world and asked them when a foetus begins the civil right to life. The answer it received is remarkable; first because it was a unanimous response by these 133 people. Second, the answer itself was remarkable: "life in the sense of historical existence of a human individual exists according to definite biological-physiological knowledge, in any case, from the fourteenth day after conception". That is even before a woman knows she is pregnant.

February 13, 1987
Right to Life
The reason they chose 14 days is because from the first day of conception through to the fourteenth day it is possible for the cells to divide into twins, triplets and so on.
I suggest that when we look at medical considerations we must remember some of these basic facts. All of them militate in one direction, which is that we recognize a foetus as a person having all the rights to life, liberty and security of person, as suggested in this motion.
Let us look at the legal considerations. According to current practice and precedent in Canadian law, a foetus is recognized for the purposes and right to sue for prenatal injury. In other words, a foetus has the right to inheritance and the right to sue for prenatal injury. Since the existing state of the law is that no legal rights attach to any person until that person has been born alive, then surely the right to life is the logical prior right on which all other rights such as the right to sue for prenatal injury depend. We do not give tonsils those rights when they are removed, but the person developing within the mother's womb is given those rights because they are considered a person. That is the purpose of this motion.
Since my time is almost up, let me conclude by quoting Major John Connors, health services consultant to the Alliance For Life. He says:
Consider, if you will, the stages of life as links in a chain. Canada's pensioners, our infirm and incapacitated, our labour force, our students, our children and, even younger, our babies, are linked together, because all are human whatever might otherwise be their status. So, too, are unborn children a link in the same chain, similarly human and even more deserving of protection because of their vulnerability. Their very weakness dictates their need of the special protection of being named under Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, which we respectfully request include a provision that everyone, from conception to natural death, has the right to life.
That is the specific point that the motion is putting before us. We are dealing with human beings. All the evidence leads to that conclusion. Let us make sure that our actions and our laws do the same thing.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak with respect to Motion No. 37, which is a genuine attempt by my colleague, the Member for Grey- Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), to extend legal rights, indeed constitutional rights, to unborn people. I must say that I rise with some trepidation because the question of abortion is one of both law and morals.
However, with the election to this Parliament comes the responsibility on each of us to consider these questions, debate them, and indeed change the law at such time as it seems appropriate to the Parliament as a whole.
The alternative is conflict in the streets, as exists in so many countries right now where people are fighting and killing each other because their political process has not worked.
I thank my colleague for bringing this question before us. It is a question that affects our nation greatly.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, under our Criminal Code, a baby is legally a person and, therefore, protected under the law only once it is out of the mother upon birth even though the umbilical cord is not cut. Out-of-womb surgery changed that idea quite dramatically in the minds of many people, in that a child can be taken out of the womb and operated on. During that period it would have all the legal rights the rest of us have. The minute it goes back into its mother, it then loses all of those rights and can be killed by a decision of a therapeutic abortion committee upon application of the mother.
It is very clear that our laws in this area have not kept pace with the advance in medical science. That is why we have an enormous group of people who want to have changes made. The real question is, when does life begin or when does one become human and, therefore, get legal protection of the law?
As with any moral question, the debate is highly emotionally charged. The reason for that is that both the pro-life and the pro-choice groups represent a very important tradition in our country. We have a long tradition on the side of the sanctity of life. We have another long tradition of freedom of choice and the right to liberty and choice. Both of these traditions are part of our western culture, going back many, many years. We cherish both of these values, and that is what makes the issue so difficult and so much of a dilemma.
For myself, I usually start with the United Nations declaration because, I believe, increasingly more and more of our young people especially are seeing the world as an integral whole and the United Nations as a legitimate attempt by society to strike common ground. Therefore, I usually start with the United Nations declaration on the rights of the child, which is a recent document published in 1959. That document states that the child, by reason of his or her physical and mental immaturity, needs special safeguards and care, including appropriate legal protection before as well as after birth.
When does a foetus become a person? Medically we know for certain that from the moment of conception the child bears an undeniable stamp of a separate, distinct person, structurally and totally different from his or her mother, with its own blood system, nervous system and genetic code. We know that four days after conception sex can be determined. Eighteen days after conception the heart tissue begins to beat. In 43 days brain waves can be detected. By the seventh week shape is umistakably human. By 10 weeks the thyroid and adrenal glands begin to function. By 12 weeks a child kicks his or her legs, turns his or her feet, curls and fans toes and so on.
I have canvassed people in my riding very carefully for seven years since becoming a Member of Parliament. I find that the women in my riding separate roughly into three groups. There are a few women, and I must say a very, very few women, who want abortion on demand right up to the moment of natural childbirth. They believe that the day before the natural childbirth, if they do not want to have the child, they do not
February 13, 1987

have to have it. I guess it would be a saline solution which would be injected which would burn the child, bringing on a miscarriage. They strongly feel they should be able to have that. However, that is just a very few women. I find that some women, a considerably larger group, believe that there should only be abortion when the mother is about to die, so it would have to be the absolute life of the mother in juxtaposition with the life of the child, and if there was a choice, the life of the mother should be chosen.
The third group, which is by far the largest group, wants birth control and not abortion. They want more research and development. They want help for young mothers. They want programs so that a pregnant woman could go in and get assistance and aid to carry that child to full term, at which time she can either put it up for adoption or decide to keep it. This group does not agree with abortion on demand. However, they do believe abortion should be available for very young women, for example, in certain instances of incest and rape and certainly in cases where the genuine health of the mother is at stake.
I find that the vast bulk of the people in my riding really fall into that category. They are not solidly pro-choice because they know there is a life there, and they are not solidly pro-life because they do see that in society, whatever its laws and principles might be, there are some situations where they themselves, despite the fact that they are good and honest Christians, Moslems, Budhists, Hindus or whatever religion, would feel that the right of the child sometimes has to give way to the right of the mother.
My own position, when I first addressed the issue superficially and quickly, was clearly pro choice. I believe now that was the easiest decision because, as a man, I have very real and deep reservations on these moral issues which primarily affect women. I think it is impossible for a man to have the sense of the terror a pregnancy can cause in women under certain circumstances. However, I must say, as I studied the issue more, as I read and thought and talked about it, my position changed. Perhaps as I get older and as I read more about the medical wonders performed, and realize just how wonderful the idea of life is, I have tended to become more pro-life than pro-choice. I have no doubt medically that life begins at conception; one cell, which I believe to be "life", divides and human form takes place very quickly. Clearly by 12 weeks it is in advanced human form and, therefore, I believe fundamentally that the current law is, after all, a human idea of the seventeenth century. Our present legal definition is really the
Right to Life
seventeenth century legal embodiment of what life is or when life achieves legal protection. With the advance in science that we have achieved we have to bring that legal definition of when a person becomes human up to modern times. It clearly goes back some considerable distance.
I, therefore, believe the solution lies in my colleagues bringing these motions, whether it is to entrench this issue in the Constitution or place it in a Private Member's Bill to amend the Criminal Code. These are all legitimate instances. I think the best way is for a parliamentary committee to study the matter. The alternative is smashing heads on the street, and I do not think that is proper. The committee should review the evidence and hear all sides of the argument and it will have to come down with a compromise, just as the seventeenth century decision was a compromise. We need to strike a compromise for the twentieth century, and certainly into the twenty-first century. I think the rights of the child have to prevail earlier in the pregnancy than they do at the moment.
In terms of principle, I am very much pro-life. I would think a committee, given a practical, hard-nosed approach, would probably come up with a line somewhere of 10 weeks to 12 weeks. Prior to that, the rights of the mother would clearly predominate in choosing between the interests of the mother and the life of the child. After that, I would think the rights would have to extend to the child. We then need the support mechanisms to help that mother carry the child through to term. I know that will not make the pro-life people happy in terms of the extremists or the pro-choice. However, we are not in this totally for principle. I know that if that became the law we would not have 65,000 abortions. There might be 2,000 or 3,000 a year. That, to me, would save tens and tens of thousands of lives, and I could live with that.
